Early New High German medical recipes (Wellcome MS.990, p. 133, verso) describing treatment of inward-turning eyelashes ('böse Haare der Augen') by means of corrosive pastes ('Corrosiff') applied to the eyelids while the patient lies stretched out on a bench, followed by three additional corrosive recipes and a healing eyewash ('Wasser nach dem Corosiff zur Haillung').

### Left Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **[Rubric] 133** | 133. The second cure is done by the corrosive and cauterization. Rub a piece of salmon flesh with 4 sinews, cut several [slits] toward the light from the front, make a through-draft like a brick or furrow thick, and lay it across the board, 2 spans long; let the patient lie on the bench straight lengthwise, stretched out, so that he lies with his neck on the folded cloth, and the head hangs over what [remains of] the cushion, and thus all extremities remain stretched out. Afterwards rub a fine, clear, fat [hen's fat / tallow?]; lift his eyelids fully up, fill his eyes therein completely full, so that the whole eyeball [is covered] or stands right, and the corrosive cannot come to the eye. Yet make it [so] that the hair does not come into the eye, but is turned completely outwards and remains so; afterwards apply the following corrosive, which you must have in readiness over a little ember. Afterwards with a little wooden/felt tube, several fine [drops] spattered on, nicely warm and fairly thick; it will begin to break [the skin] around the eyes, so let him lie thus for a while or half an hour on the cushion; afterwards wipe the corrosive cleanly away again with a little sponge or soft cloth, so that nothing remains hanging on the eyelids, nor anything thereof melts into the eye [where] you must scratch the handful away. When everything is cleanly washed/wiped away, rub the [fat] out of the eye again, and use the water which I describe [for] the healing of the corrosive. *— Note: Page number '133' boxed in red ink at upper left; red ruling lines frame the text block and divide the two columns. Standard 17th-century Kurrentschrift with rubricated headings in red ink. Recto folio (p. 134) in a two-column layout detailing the third surgical cure for trichiasis ('Die drite Chur ist. die har sambt den fleisch Hinwegh Zue Schneiden'), involving suturing and excising the eyelid margin, followed by post-operative poultice/plaster care using egg white and a mineral/gold-marked ingredient, a warning to operate while the patient is fasting, and a powder recipe for proud flesh ('Ein Puluer Zum überigen fleisch'). The right column features a large watercolor anatomical/surgical illustration of a face with blood dripping from both eyes and a curved needle/lancet at the left eye.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Surgical illustration of eyelid incision and bleeding** (`#xywh=2450,1440,2150,2880`): Watercolor portrait of a young person's head with shoulder-length curly brown hair, facing forward. Vertical red streaks of blood drip from both lower eyelids down the cheeks. A dark curved surgical needle or lancet is positioned at the upper margin of the patient's left eye (viewer's right), illustrating the suturing and excision of the eyelid.

A large rubbed/water-stained patch obscures parts of lines 8–11 in the left column. Rubricated headings are written in red ink. The symbol ☉ (Sol) in line 37 appears as a circle with a central dot.* |

Thereafter take a surgical suture needle (Heftnadel) threaded with a red [...] silk thread; thereafter take a suture cannula (Heftröhrlein), gently lift the eyelid, and pierce it with the suture needle. Pull the thread through and cut it off so that it hangs a finger's length at both ends, as the following figure clearly shows you. Such piercing should be done 3 times on each eyelid, or 4 times; then grasp all 3 or 4 threads in one hand and draw the eyelid evenly forward. Hold it thus evenly elevated, and with the other hand take the scissors and cut evenly behind the thread from one corner to the other, and take great care that you do not cut outside the corner of the eye-angles and leave no hair-stump standing; and the eyelid should be cut away evenly up to the width of 2 knife-backs, so that the hair roots are removed everywhere, and it is properly done thereafter. |

Conclusion of a preceding wound-healing treatment, followed by a section on 'flashes and fire-flames of the eyes' (photopsia / early cataract or black star) attributed to overloaded ocular humors and congealed blood, treated with purgation, vesicatories behind the ears (illustrated), herbal decoctions, a head wash, distilled eye water, and an eye plaster.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Vesicatoria behind the ears** (`#xywh=3280,580,2180,2140`): Watercolor illustration of the back of a man's curly brown head showing two rectangular white blistering plasters (vesicatoria) applied behind the left and right ears, bounded below by a red horizontal rule.

Continuation of the eye plaster recipe and an eye ointment for the preceding condition, followed by a detailed surgical treatise on fused eyelids ('Zusamen gewachsne augen' / ankyloblepharon), describing how to separate the upper and lower eyelids with a suture needle, silk thread, knife, and scissors, illustrated with a portrait of a woman with closed eyes, and post-operative dressing with charpie.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Closed eyelids of a woman** (`#xywh=2460,1970,2460,2710`): Watercolor portrait of a woman's face with closed eyes, dark curly hair adorned with red ribbons/bows, and a gold band and red bead necklace, illustrating fused/closed eyelids above a red horizontal dividing rule.

Treatise on 'growths of the eyes' ('Von den Gewächßen der augen'), describing benign/fatty eyelid tumors and their surgical excision using a suture thread, small knife, and scissors (illustrated with a man's face showing bleeding eyelid tumors pierced by threads), followed by post-operative dressing with egg white, water, and tow, and a wound-healing ointment recipe ('Ain guettes Salbel Zue den geschnidtenen augen gewächß').

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Excision of eyelid growths** (`#xywh=3140,300,2380,2800`): Watercolor portrait of a mustachioed and goateed man's face with two large round reddish growths protruding from both eyelids, each pierced by suture threads and dripping blood down his cheeks, bounded below by a red-orange horizontal rule.

Recto page 138 in two columns: 'Von Geschwerlein der augen gersten oder habern genand' (On small ulcers/styes of the eyes, called barleycorns or oats). Describes styes/chalazia on the upper and lower eyelids, accompanied by a large watercolor portrait of a man's face with stylized black geometric facial hair and inflamed/swollen eyelids. Followed by causes (salted thick blood and viscous phlegm), a poultice ('die Erste Khur. ain Vmbschlag'), an ointment ('Ain andere Guete Salben'), two plasters ('Ain Guettes Pflaster dargüe', 'Ain Anders'), and instructions for surgical incision if salves and plasters fail.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Eye Stye / Hordeolum Portrait** (`#xywh=180,1580,2200,2770`): Watercolor portrait of a man with brown curly hair, stylized black geometric moustache and goatee patches, and swollen reddish upper eyelids illustrating eye styes ('gersten oder habern').

Verso page 139 in two columns: Continuation of surgical procedure for eye styes (threading with a curved needle and silk thread, incising lengthwise, pressing out fluid, dressing with egg white). Followed by a new chapter: 'Von den Waser Galln der augen. oder gewachs der augen' (On water-galls or growths of the eyes / Atheromata), with a recipe for 'Ein Sehr guette Confecto Salben' containing killed mercury, surgical excision instructions, a watercolor portrait ('Figur der Waser Gall') showing bilateral swollen eyelid cysts, and post-operative dressing with digestive ointment and mercury precipitate.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Figur der Waser Gall** (`#xywh=2820,3350,2460,2570`): Watercolor portrait of a man with brown curly hair, thin moustache and goatee, displaying two large round fluid-filled swellings ('water galls' / atheromata) on both upper eyelids.

Recto page 140 in two columns: Completion of the water-gall healing instructions, followed by a new chapter: 'Von den Zittern vnd Vippern der augen Glidern' (On trembling and twitching of the eyelids). Discusses intermittent, continuous, hereditary, and convulsive eyelid twitching and their humoral/windy causes, followed by internal and external remedies: two herbal drinks ('Ain Guets Tranckh', 'Ain anders Tranckh'), a head wash ('Ain guete haubt Waschung'), two eye waters ('Ain Guetes Waser', 'Ain anders Waser'), an eyelid salve ('Ain guets Sälbel'), a snuff powder ('Ain guets Schnupf Puluor'), and dietary/regimen warnings (avoiding solitude, late suppers, cold/moist foods, and fog).

Remedies and dietary regimen for burned and injured eyes, including a verbena-water and quince-seed mucilage poultice, poppy-seed and olive-oil salve for raw flesh, houseleek and terra sigillata eye drops, and a breast-milk and rose-water wash.

Full-page coloured illustration of a Franciscan apothecary's eye-remedy dispensary framed by an architectural arch, showing five shelves of labelled eye medicines (pills, powders, ointments, waters, confections) and a friar handing a bottle to a blindfolded patient.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Apothecary Eye Dispensary** (`#xywh=190,110,4610,5510`): Full-page coloured pen-and-ink wash illustration framed by two blue marbled columns and a yellow-and-grey stone arch. Five yellow shelves hold rows of apothecary vessels under hanging signs: Augen Pilule (11 red cylindrical jars), Augen Puluer (10 red jars), Augen salben (8 blue-and-white ceramic albarelli), Augen waser (7 square glass bottles), and Augen Confect (12 red jars). Below, a tonsured Franciscan friar in a brown habit with a rosary hands a small bottle to a blindfolded gentleman holding a hat and walking stick, while two more blindfolded patients with sticks enter through a doorway on the left. A framed chart hangs on the back wall and a table on the right holds apothecary vessels.

Introduction to the 'Apothecary of the Poor' for ocular remedies, followed by an illustration of two pillboxes and nine recipes for ophthalmic and cephalic purgative pills (pilulae lucis maiores, cochiarum, sine quibus esse nolo, aurearum, de succino Cratonis, etc.).

**Two Pillboxes** (`#xywh=830,2040,2280,670`): Coloured pen-and-ink wash illustration on a yellow background band showing two round ribbed wooden or earthenware pillboxes filled with dark spherical pills.

Two-column page containing recipes for purging pills (especially for head and rheumy eye pains, including 'ascarisch Pillule'), laxative powders, an illustration of five colored apothecary flasks for eye waters, and a recipe for red and running eyes.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Five Eye-Water Flasks** (`#xywh=2560,4190,2110,720`): Row of five rectangular/octagonal colored apothecary bottles or flasks with stoppers (reddish-purple, blue, pink, tan, dark blue-green) standing on a brown shelf beneath the heading for various eye waters.

Verso folio (p. 147) in two columns containing ophthalmic recipes: a cataplasm for barleycorns (styes) on the eye, a wondrous eye-water for all fluxes and strengthening vision distilled per alembicum in a Balneum Mariae, additional eye-waters (including pike gall, celandine, valerian, eyebright), remedies for 'flies' before the eyes, incipient cataracts (starn), hot eye fluxes, and films/spots (fell und maill).

Verso folio (p. 149) in two columns titled 'Von Underschiedlichen augen Sälblen' (On various eye ointments), featuring a watercolor illustration of four apothecary ointment jars on a shelf at the top of the left column. Recipes cover ointments for heated/inflamed eye pains (tutia, coral, Armenian bole, white lead, fresh unsalted butter, hematite, pearls) and in the right column ointments for eye fistulas (with copaiba balsam), pain-stilling (quince seeds, roasted apples, sugar of lead), eye ulcers, inflammation/pustules, and a cataplasm for eye inflammation.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Four Apothecary Ointment Jars** (`#xywh=830,920,2270,740`): Watercolor illustration of four apothecary jars/pots arranged in a row on a brown shelf: from left to right, a white/grey bulbous jar, a reddish-brown jar, a yellow-ochre lidded jar, and a pinkish-red handled pitcher.

Treatises on ocular films, spots, and blemishes (fell, fleckhen, maill der augen), especially for the poor and elderly. Includes dietary and humoral regimen (avoiding sadness, weeping, smoke, bloodletting, cold, wind, dust, pond fish, pork, dairy, waterfowl, and damp air), internal remedies (medicinal salt, herbal decoctions, purging pills), and external applications (ant-oil distillation, celandine water, gold/alumen, honey, and egg-yolk oil). Illustrated with a watercolor of a human eye showing a corneal opacity.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Fig. 1** (`#xywh=640,1130,850,530`): Watercolor drawing in a rectangular ink frame depicting a human eye with a brown iris and a white spot/opacity (fell/fleck) on the cornea/pupil.

Collection of ophthalmic waters, powders (trisenet), and collyria for eye films and blemishes. Includes a complex eye water with pike and sheep gall, a strengthening digestive powder (trisenet), a tutia-and-malmsey collyrium aged in the sun, a sky-blue copper/vitriol water, sharp eye waters, a ripe strawberry fermentation remedy, a candle-soot insufflation, and an astrological/sympathetic dandelion root amulet dug at St. Bartholomew's Day.

Remedies for eye soreness/corners and ocular blisters or pustules (Bladtern in augen). Includes fennel-herb wine, purgative head pills with grayling fat (äsch schmalz), leaf-on-anvil dew, peeled beans in wine, red mugwort root worn on the arm, hard-boiled eggs in vinegar, and ginger with egg white. Dominated by a large central watercolor scene of a bearded monk surgeon operating on the eye of a reclining gentleman.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Fig. 2** (`#xywh=430,2200,4250,3850`): Full-width watercolor scene depicting a bearded friar/monk surgeon in a brown habit performing an eye operation with a small instrument on a male patient in a blue coat and red breeches lying on a wooden bench/bed. To the left is an apothecary shelf with red jars, colored glass bottles, and a table with flasks; behind is an open wooden door and a leaded-glass window on the right.

Page 153 (verso), two columns. Left column features three watercolor/ink illustrations of ophthalmic instruments (two round-headed/sponge-tipped probes and one blue-grey double-ended probe with two eyed/ringed instruments below), followed by recipes for eyes struck or bruised, 'wild flesh' (pterygium) in the eyes, and blisters/pustules forming films. Right column continues the blister/film remedy, then gives a compound eye powder ('Puluer') for failing sight or brain weakness, a remedy for films ('fell der augen'), and a hen-fat and honey ointment for spots/maculae in the eye.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Ophthalmic probes and specula/applicators** (`#xywh=850,440,2340,2170`): Three horizontal instrument drawings in the upper left column: (1) a brown rod with a stippled, round sponge- or brush-like head at the left end; (2) a brown rod with a similar stippled round head at the right end; (3) a blue-grey double-ended probe/cannula with two small blue-grey eyed/ringed instruments (possibly eye specula or trocars/guards) drawn directly beneath it.

Page 154 (recto), two columns, no illustrations. Left column contains ophthalmic remedies for holding back eye fluxes (hot hard-boiled egg on the neck), obstructed eye nerves (tormentil plaster), foreign bodies in the eye (eye-pearls), pain and inflammation (roasted apple, egg-white, and Armenian bole salve), dim eyes (fennel herb), and sight lost from smallpox (pimpernel juice). Right column contains remedies for a membrane/film growing over the eyes (myrrh in white rose water), hot eyes (linden blossom water), childhood cataract (pike gall with sugar), eye films (antimony and haematite powder), weeping eyes (egg-white and salt water), and incipient cataract (coarse rose water), which continues onto Page 155.

Page 155 (verso), two columns with illustrations in both columns. Left column finishes the cataract water from p. 154, shows three circular golden-brown lozenges/troches, and gives recipes for masticatories for weeping eyes, head-strengthening lozenges ('Haubt stärckhente Zeltel'), another lozenge for catarrhal head, and head pills for eye weakness. Right column finishes the head pills, illustrates eight conical and disc-shaped 'Sief' collyria, and gives recipes for 'Sief album Rasis', 'Sief album sine opio', 'Sief de Rosis', and 'Sief de Thure'.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Masticatory lozenges / troches** (`#xywh=960,890,1410,410`): Three circular golden-brown lozenges or troches drawn in a row below the opening continuation lines in the left column; the first two show six-spoked wheel/star markings, while the third is plain stippled brown-gold.

**Sief collyria forms (cones and discs)** (`#xywh=3270,960,2140,480`): Eight dark grey-brown drawings of Sief collyria/troches arranged in a horizontal row above the 'Sief' rubric in the right column: three pointed cones on the left, three circular discs in the middle, and two pointed cones on the right.

Recto folio (Page 156) in two columns containing ophthalmic recipes: Sief de Chalcantho, Sief Viride, a cooling milk eye-wash used in Austria, and three eye ointments (Augen Sälbel) accompanied by an illustration of a blue-grey glazed apothecary jar on a yellow base.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Apothecary Ointment Jar** (`#xywh=2850,580,1000,770`): Coloured drawing of a blue-grey glazed ceramic apothecary jar resting on a yellow/ochre oval base at the top of the right column.

### Left Column

| 3 | Thue ihn in den ✚ , vnd laß halb einsiede[n] | Put it into the crucible, and let it boil down by half, *— Note: ✚ here clearly denotes a crucible or vessel ('in den ✚').* |
| 4 | als dan thue darzue 2 . ℥ . nuc[is] miristi= | then add thereto 2 ounces of nutmeg, *— Note: Abbreviated 'nuc[is] miristi=' (nux myristica), hyphenated across lines 4–5.* |

Verso folio (Page 157) in two columns featuring forehead plasters/powders ('Pulver auf die Stiern') with an illustration of a head bound with a blue forehead bandage, followed by collyria ('Colirio optalmico', 'Coliro albo') and an illustration of a green cylindrical apothecary jar on a yellow base.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Bandaged Head** (`#xywh=1150,930,1500,1470`): Coloured drawing of a young person's head with curled hair and a blue cloth bandage tied around the forehead with a bow on the left, above a horizontal scroll/bar.

**Green Cylindrical Apothecary Jar** (`#xywh=1350,4950,850,950`): Coloured drawing of a green cylindrical apothecary vessel/jar resting on a yellow/ochre oval base in the lower left column.

Verso folio (p. 159) in two columns containing ophthalmic recipes: continuation of an eye-water recipe, powders and electuaries to strengthen weak eyesight (using eyebright, valerian, galangal, spikenard, cubebs, and pearls), and two compound eye-waters (including pike gall, malmsey wine, and tutia).

Recto folio (p. 160) in two columns covering incipient white cataracts (with mouse blood, sarcocolla, vulture/dove gall, and Peruvian balsam), weeping/running eyes (epiphora, with forehead plasters and vesicatories), everted/swollen eyelids (ectropion/edema), eye abscesses/ulcers (with sugar of lead and corneal puncture), and wasting of the eyebrows.

### Left Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |

| 2 | **[Rubric] starn.** | cataract. *— Note: Red-ink rubric.* |
| 3 | Wan im anfang des weisen starn. Müeß das flüs= | When at the beginning of white cataract, specks/flocculi *— Note: flüs= hyphenated.* |
| 4 | seben Vor den augen scheinen, so brauch Volgentes | appear floating before the eyes, use the following *— Note: seben = schweben.* |

Ophthalmological recipes and treatments: calamine and tutty collyria, a discussion of eye inflammation (Entzündung der Augen) with bloodletting, leeches, and poultices, followed by a treatise on films and spots of the eyes (Von Fell und Mail der Augen) including a vitriol/sugar of lead collyrium, roasted apple cataplasm, antimonial ophthalmic water (aqua ophthalmica antimonialis), and burnt swallow's head with honey.

### Left Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |

Colored illustration of two gesturing men above a red-ink title introducing a series of medical-optical questions and answers ('Volgen Etliche Schöne fragstück Von den gesicht vnd den augen'), covering tearing during laughing/drinking, poor sight with clear eyes, farsightedness in deep-set vs. large eyes, aging vision, eye movement fatigue, double vision when pressing one eye, myopia/presbyopia, and night vision.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Two men gesturing in conversation** (`#xywh=980,420,2240,1700`): Colored watercolor/ink illustration at top left above the title: on the left, a man in a white cap and beige/brown robe gesturing toward the right; on the right, a man in a red plumed hat, yellow doublet, and blue breeches gesturing toward the left, standing on grassy ground.

Verso folio (page 165, written '1.65' in a red-ruled box at upper left) in two columns containing a physiognomic and humoral-medical catechism (red-ink 'Warumb' questions with brown/black-ink 'Weillen/Weill' answers) concerning the eyes and eyebrows: red eyes and weak sight, fixed/immovable eyes and deep thoughts, darting vs. slow eyes and complexion/intelligence, clear eyes and unfaithfulness, small eyes and gall/wickedness, blinking and weak eyes, swollen eyes and moist brain/sleepiness, incomplete closure of lower eyelids and short life, thick eyebrows near the nose and wrathful nature, eyes suffering cold due to bad blood, and parted eyebrows indicating cold/moist timidity.

### Left Column

| 8 | **[Rubric] sind tieffsin[n]ige gedanck[en].** | of deep thoughts? *— Note: Nasal bar over 'n' in 'tieffsin[n]ige'; -en loop on 'gedanck[en]'.* |

Full-page plate of watercolor and ink illustrations (page 166 in red-ruled box at upper right; small ink plate number '64' at lower left) divided by red ruling lines into six compartments depicting alchemical and pharmaceutical distillation apparatus: baths, retorts, pelicans, a serpentine/zigzag fractionating column, crossed-spout alembics, a tiered filter/fire-bath stand, brick distillation furnaces, and receivers.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Upper-Left Distillation Vessels** (`#xywh=150,280,2300,1370`): Three vessels: a round-bottomed flask seated in a cylindrical vessel with radiating lines at top; a blue-tinted glass retort/alembic with side spout; and a blue-tinted two-handled circulatory vessel (pelican).

**Upper-Right Serpentine Distillation Train** (`#xywh=2450,280,2200,3420`): Brown earthenware cucurbit with a tall zigzag/serpentine ascending condenser column and alembic head discharging into a tilted blue glass receiver set in a funnel-topped pedestal, fed simultaneously by a tall blue-tinted matrass-alembic on the right.

**Middle-Left Tripod Vat and Crossed-Spout Alembics** (`#xywh=150,1700,2300,2100`): At left, a three-legged stand over a small blue flask and fire supporting a coopered vat, cloth strainer, and top dish of red-orange coals/herbs with a long handle; at right, two blue glass alembics with crossed spouts.

**Middle-Right Conical Hood and Bath-Seated Vessel** (`#xywh=2300,3480,2250,1270`): At left, a horizontal conical blue glass hood/funnel with two spouts; at right, a faceted blue glass vessel seated inside a round brown earthenware bath dish.

**Lower-Left Brick Furnace and Circulatory Flask** (`#xywh=150,3850,2250,2350`): At left, a brick-built furnace with arched firebox heating a bath and blue glass alembic whose spout drains into a small receiver on an adjacent plinth; at right, a tall pear-shaped blue glass matrass/circulatory flask.

**Lower-Right Brick Furnace with Stool-Mounted Receiver** (`#xywh=2420,4750,2130,1730`): A brick furnace with arched firebox heating a copper/brown retort whose spout leads into a brown earthenware receiver jar resting on a four-legged wooden stool, with a small pot beneath.

Full-page plate of watercolor and ink illustrations (page 167, written '1.67' in a red-ruled box at upper left; small ink number '67' at lower right) divided by olive-brown ruling lines into six compartments depicting alchemical and pharmaceutical distillation and separation apparatus: bath-seated alembics, a large earthenware retort with blue receiver, a copper condenser vat with spigot and amphora receiver, stepped brick cascade syphon setups, multi-bulbed aludel column, and a brick furnace with a wooden cooling barrel (worm tub).

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Upper-Left Alembic in Bath and Earthenware Retort** (`#xywh=920,380,2230,1470`): At left, a blue glass alembic seated in a yellow-brown bath ring; at right, a large brown earthenware retort with long curving neck discharging into a blue glass long-necked receiver.

**Upper-Right Spigoted Condenser Vat and Receivers** (`#xywh=3180,400,2200,2550`): A large copper/brown funnel-shaped vat with a side spigot mounted atop a two-handled brown earthenware jug; a tilted blue glass flask on a tall wooden stand feeds in at left, while a tall blue-grey two-handled amphora catches the outflow at right.

**Middle-Left Stepped Cascade, Double Pot, and Bath Flask** (`#xywh=920,1850,2230,2830`): A five-tier brick stepped cascade with cups linked by red overflow tubes into a tilted glass flask; a two-part brown earthenware stacked vessel (aludel/digestion pot) at right; and a pear-shaped spouted vessel in a yellow-brown bath ring below.

**Middle-Right Multi-Bulbed Column and Paired Alembics** (`#xywh=3180,2950,2200,1900`): Three blue-tinted glass vessels: a four-bulbed fractionating/aludel column with alembic head at left, a pear-shaped alembic in the center, and a conical-bodied alembic at right with crossing spouts.

**Lower-Left Brick Furnace with Wooden Cooling Barrel** (`#xywh=920,4680,2230,1770`): A square brick furnace with arched firebox and square vent topped by a dark copper still whose long spout passes through a coopered wooden cooling barrel (worm tub) on a four-legged stand.

**Lower-Right Stepped Cascade and Gourd Vessel** (`#xywh=3180,4850,2200,1600`): At left, a three-tier brick stepped cascade with shallow bowls linked by red overflow streams into a small tilted glass receiver; at right, a tall double-bellied brown earthenware gourd-shaped vessel.

Recto leaf (p. 168) with three watercolor illustrations of distillation and alchemical furnaces/apparatuses (two in the left column, one at the top of the right column), followed in the lower right column by a red-ink rubric and 24 lines of Early New High German definitions of alchemical and distillation operations.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Double-alembic water/sand-bath furnace** (`#xywh=200,550,2050,3450`): Watercolor illustration of a cylindrical brick furnace on three legs with a square fire-door, topped by a round wooden-staved bath vessel holding two blue-gray alembics/retorts with spouts.

**Barrel-bath alembic furnace** (`#xywh=500,4020,1550,2480`): Watercolor illustration of a square/box-like furnace base supporting a cylindrical bath and a wooden-staved barrel vessel containing a blue-gray cucurbit and alembic head.

**Brick retort/alembic furnace with receiver** (`#xywh=2380,310,2070,1810`): Watercolor illustration of a rectangular brick furnace with an arched fire-door, topped by a blue-gray alembic whose spout leads into a tilted blue-gray receiver flask resting on a four-legged wooden stand.

### Left Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |

### Right Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **[Rubric] Etliche Stück die in der distelation** | Several items [procedures] that in distillation *— Note: Red-ink rubric heading.* |
| 2 | **[Rubric] gebraucht werden** | are used. *— Note: Continuation of red-ink rubric heading.* |
| 3 | Per ascensum . durchß aufsteigen . | Per ascensum: by ascending. *— Note: Distillation by ascent.* |
| 4 | Balneo Vaporosa dampff bad . | Balneo vaporoso: steam bath. *— Note: Latin 'balneum vaporosum' (vapor bath).* |
| 5 | Per de liquiam . wie daß ▽ so gemacht | Per deliquium: how the water [liquid] is thus made *— Note: Glyph resembles alchemical water/liquid sign (▽) or oil/salt; 'wird' added supralinearly at end of line 6.* |
| 6 | per medium Cornutum . ‹wird› | Per medium cornutum [is made]: *— Note: Supralinear 'wird' at right completes the clause from line 5.* |
| 7 | durch dʒ krumpe rodorten . | through the crooked retort. *— Note: dʒ = 'das'; 'rodorten' = Retorte (retort).* |
| 8 | Per descensum . vnder sich geht . | Per descensum: goes downward. *— Note: Distillation by descent.* |
| 9 | Sublimare . erhöht wird . | Sublimare: is elevated. *— Note: Sublimation.* |
| 10 | Rectification . er förcht den Rauch | Rectification: it fears [avoids/purifies] the smoke/vapor *— Note: Or 'er höcht' / 'er förcht'; context refers to redistilling to make a substance purer.* |
| 11 | daß ein ding reiner vn geistiger wird ob | so that a thing becomes purer and more spirituous, whether *— Note: 'vn' with abbreviation stroke = 'und'.* |
| 12 | es in der Retortn oder im Kholbn . | it be in the retort or in the flask [cucurbit]. *— Note: 'Kholbn' = Kolben.* |
| 13 | Coagulirn ein dickhen . | Coagulating: a thickening. *— Note: Coagulation.* |
| 14 | dulcoration auß süessen . | Dulcoration: sweetening out. *— Note: Washing away acridity/salts.* |
| 15 | Inclination abgiessen . | Inclination: pouring off [decanting]. *— Note: Decantation by tilting the vessel.* |
| 16 | Amalgamirung Vermischung . | Amalgamation: mixing together. *— Note: Combining metals (especially with mercury).* |
| 17 | Digestion ein sanffte durchdringung | Digestion: a gentle permeation *— Note: Gentle prolonged heating/maturation.* |
| 18 | Putrefaction . fäulung . ‹wärme› | Putrefaction: rotting / decay [warmth]. *— Note: 'wärme' written in smaller hand to the right, possibly completing 'durchdringung' or glossing gentle heat.* |
| 19 | Menstruo ist ein auf lösete feüchtigk: | Menstruum is a dissolving moisture [solvent]. *— Note: 'feüchtigk:' = Feuchtigkeit.* |
| 20 | Circulation ist ein auf vnd absteigen | Circulation is an ascending and descending *— Note: Refluxing in a circulatory vessel.* |
| 21 | in MB: ☉ mit feüchter 🜖 . | in a water bath [balneum Mariae] with moist [vapor/vessel]. *— Note: 'MB:' = Mariae Balneo; followed by circular symbol (☉) and an alembic/double-bulb glyph (represented as 🜖).* |
| 22 | Reuerberiern Verbrenen in 2 Verschlossen | Reverberating: burning in two closed [vessels] *— Note: Or 'in z[u] verschlossen' (in a closed furnace/vessel).* |
| 23 | Calciniern in offnen geschir werd ‹geschier› | Calcining: in an open vessel. *— Note: 'geschier' added/repeated above right.* |
| 24 | Stratification ein geleg ‹eins› auf dʒ ander | Stratification: a laying one upon another. *— Note: Stratum super stratum; 'eins' added supralinearly.* |
| 25 | decrepitation Verpröffen . | Decrepitation: crackling / bursting in fire. *— Note: Heating salts until they cease crackling.* |
| 26 | Cohobation das wider holte holte | Cohobation: the repeated [distillation]. *— Note: Final word 'holte' repeated with flourish.* |

Recto leaf (p. 170, marked '1.70' in upper right) featuring a large top-half watercolor illustration of a sickroom scene (bearded patient in bed, physician, weeping woman, draped table, open door), above two columns of Early New High German prognostic medical text on signs of life or death from sweat, the eyes, and the face.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Sickroom scene** (`#xywh=200,220,4350,2430`): Watercolor illustration spanning the full page width: a bare-chested bearded patient under a green blanket in a carved wooden bed on the left; a long-haired physician gesturing between the patient and a standing weeping woman holding a handkerchief to her eyes; a green-draped table with vessels and plates, a four-paned window, and an open wooden door on the right.

### Left Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **[Rubric] Kenzeichen Zum Leben oder** | Signs of life or *— Note: Large red-ink rubric heading.* |
| 2 | **[Rubric] Tott eines Krancken ~** | death of a sick person. *— Note: Continuation of large red-ink rubric heading.* |
| 3 | **[Rubric] Kenzeichen auß dem Schweiß .** | Signs from sweat. *— Note: Red-ink section rubric.* |
| 4 | In allen starcken Kranckheiten hat man aufsehen | In all severe illnesses one must pay attention *— Note: 'aufsehen' (or 'Ansehen') = regard/observation.* |
| 5 | auß die gesund . wan er in den Bösen tägen | to the health; when he, in the evil [critical] days, *— Note: 'auß' likely for 'auf'.* |
| 6 | kombt . vnd der Kranckheit den lauff auß sind . | arrives, and the course of the illness is upon them; *— Note: 'auß sind' = 'auf sind' / 'aus sind'.* |
| 7 | ein Schweiß der Kalt Vnßerzeit kombt . vn kalt | a sweat that comes cold [and] untimely, and is cold *— Note: 'Vnßerzeit' / 'Vnbezeit' = untimely/unseasonable.* |
| 8 | ist . vnd allein Vmb das hertz schwitzt . die sind nit | and sweats only around the heart, those are not *— Note: Cold sweat around the precordia as a grave prognostic sign.* |
| 9 | gütt . | good. |
| 10 | Wan ein mensch in großer schwachheit ligt , vnd schwitzt | When a person lies in great weakness, and sweats |
| 11 | Vmb die Nasen kalt schweiß . dieses ist tötlich . | cold sweat around the nose, this is fatal. |
| 12 | Sonderlich auch der Athem der aufsteütt kalte . | Especially also when the breath that rises up is cold, *— Note: 'aufsteütt' = aufsteigt.* |
| 13 | so die Nasen gespitzet sind . | when the nose is pinched [pointed]. *— Note: Classical Hippocratic facies sign.* |
| 14 | Wan der schweiß Vmb den hals allein , vnd im ange= | When the sweat is around the neck alone, and in the face *— Note: Hyphenated across line break to 'sicht'.* |
| 15 | sicht , vnd der Nasen . ist es böß . | and the nose, it is bad. |
| 16 | Wan der schweiß Troffen weiß geht . vn am | When the sweat comes drop-wise, and on the *— Note: 'Troffen weiß' = tropfenweise.* |
| 17 | ganzen leib . als der ganze leib warm ist | whole body, while the whole body is warm, |
| 18 | dieses ist güet . auf das der schweiß darmit | this is good, so that the sweat thereby |
| 19 | den schmerzen dan bey vnd starck wird . Welches | is present with the pain and becomes strong; which |
| 20 | nach dem schwitzen sich löste vn ringern sich befind | after sweating loosens itself and finds itself eased. *— Note: 'ringern' = verringern (diminish/ease).* |
| 21 | dieses zeigt an . das der mensch will feüchtigkeit | This indicates that the person has much moisture *— Note: 'will' = viel (much).* |
| 22 | bey sich hat . vn die Natur den überfluß von sich | within himself, and nature drives the excess from itself |
| 23 | treibt . ~ | out. |
| 24 | Wan ein Mensch allein Vmb das hertz schwitzt | When a person sweats only around the heart, *— Note: Sentence continues at top of Right Column.* |

### Right Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | so ist ein Zeichen , das der mensch sehr widerwertig | then it is a sign that the person is very contrary *— Note: Continuation from Left Column line 24.* |
| 2 | in der Natur ist . oder das die Natur zuviel | in his nature, or that nature is too much |
| 3 | erkalt . vnd schwach ist . vn mit sanfftheit zü den | cooled, and is weak, and with gentleness to |
| 4 | Schweiß schon auß treiben — , | drive out the sweat gently. *— Note: 'schon' (or 'thun' = tun).* |
| 5 | **[Rubric] Kenzeichen auß den augen .** | Signs from the eyes. *— Note: Red-ink section rubric.* |
| 6 | Wan die krancken das liecht scheuhen . die augen | When the sick shun the light; the eyes *— Note: Photophobia.* |
| 7 | verkeern . das eins auch kliner . das weiße im | roll/turn; that one [eye] is also smaller; the white in the *— Note: 'kliner' = kleiner (smaller).* |
| 8 | aug rod wird . die backen er bläichen . die | eye becomes red; the cheeks grow pale; the *— Note: 'rod' = rot; 'er bläichen' = erbleichen.* |
| 9 | äderlen darin schwartz werden . die augen | little veins therein become black; the eyes *— Note: 'äderlen' = Äderlein.* |
| 10 | offt auf vnd zü thuen . groß auf schauen . | often open and shut; stare wide open; |

| 15 | scheindt . Welches Vor malen nit in gewohn= | shines, which previously was not in habit *— Note: Hyphenated across line break to 'heit'.* |
| 16 | heit gehabt . ist ein bößes Zeichen . | [had not been habitual], is a bad sign. |

| 18 | In gefahrlichen Kranckheiten müß man das | In dangerous illnesses one must |

| 21 | noch einem gesünden gleich sicht oder nit . | still looks like a healthy person or not. |

| 23 | heüte ein gezogene ohren , d Nasen ein gefallen | [and] skin, drawn-in ears, the nose fallen in, *— Note: 'heüte' = Häute; 'd' = die.* |
| 24 | sind schleime Zeichen . | are bad signs. *— Note: 'schleime' = schlimme.* |
| 25 | Wan die haüt hart eben auf der stirn glat | When the skin is hard, even, smooth on the forehead |

| 27 | grün bleich ist blaw oder bley farb . diß | is pale green, blue, or lead-colored, this *— Note: 'ist' (or 'sie'); sentence continues on following leaf.* |

Verso folio (p. 173) containing a spirited Baroque medical polemic comparing the 'Ancients' (die Alten) and the 'Moderns' (die Jungen Ärzte) on bloodletting theory (choosing specific veins like the cephalic, median, hepatic, or saphenous vs. letting blood from any convenient vein) and on astrological/lunar calendar signs.

Continuation of rules for bloodletting (Aderlass): preliminary purging of the body, avoiding eating/drinking immediately after phlebotomy, warnings against excessive bloodletting weakening the stomach and vital spirits, seasonal timing (summer), resting afterwards, proper incision size and volume (5 to 8 or 10 ounces), and critique of superficial blood-bowl examination.

Critique of unnecessary bloodletting and defense of the author's caution; followed by anatomical descriptions of nerves (Sennadern, spiritus animales), tendons (Spannadern, tendines), lacteal vessels (Milchadern, chylus, ductus thoracicus), and lymphatic vessels (Vasa Lymphatica) including salivary, biliary (ductus biliarius), and lacrimal ducts.

Conclusion on lacrimal ducts; section on veins and arteries (Blut- und Pulsadern) suitable for opening, critique of excessive French bloodletting (case of a cavalier who fell from his horse), comparison with more sparing German practice, watercolor illustration of varicose veins on the legs, and treatise 'Von den Kropff oder Krampff adern' (varicose veins).

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Varicose Veins (Krampfadern) Illustration** (`#xywh=2560,1810,2160,1700`): Watercolor and ink anatomical illustration of a seated figure's lower body in yellow breeches with bare legs, showing prominent, tortuous, dark red-purple varicose veins (Krampfadern) along the calves and shins, resting on a horizontal ground line.

Medical treatments for moist coldness/putrid ulcers, bloodletting and bandaging of the legs/feet to draw blood upward, treatment of inflamed varicose veins (krampff aderen) with herbal decoctions and a poultice/cushion (Kisen), and a rubricated section on varicocele (swollen spermatic veins in the scrotum) caused by sharp melancholic blood.

Large watercolor illustration of a sick bearded friar in bed attended by another friar bringing food and medicine on a tray, followed by a rubricated chapter on nursing the sick, diet, and the proper timing and administration of purgatives and medicines.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Sickbed Nursing Scene** (`#xywh=150,190,4490,3470`): Watercolor illustration in a black-ruled frame showing a bearded, tonsured friar in a brown habit lying in a wooden bed under a white coverlet. Beside the bed is a small wooden chair with a heart-shaped cutout, and behind it a table with an hourglass, a book, a crucifix, apothecary jars, and a cup. On the right, a second friar enters through an open doorway carrying a white-draped tray with a pitcher and five bowls.

Dietary regimen and nursing care for fever patients, illustrated with a framed watercolor of a bearded man seated at a table with food and drink. The text covers when to withhold or give food, the importance of small portions and clean preparation, forbidden and recommended foods in tertian fevers (barley, panada, almond milk, roasted apples, boiled plums, rice, borage, verjuice), and avoiding overly hot food.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Wie man die khranckhe in fieber mit Essen vnd Trinckhen halten Soll** (`#xywh=350,500,2312,1800`): Framed watercolor illustration showing a bearded man in a brown robe seated at a wooden table in a room with a framed picture on the wall. On the table are plates of food, bread, a knife, and a pewter pitcher and cup.

Continuation on drinks for fever patients (barley water, hartshorn, sorrel root, wine forbidden except in quartans), followed by theoretical treatises on what fever is (unnatural heat affecting vital spirits, humors, and blood), why fevers recur at different intervals (quotidian, tertian, quartan) based on humor thickness, and an analysis of legitimate/exquisite tertian fever.

Symptoms and treatment of tertian fever, including cooling syrups (chicory, endive, sorrel, borage, burnet-saxifrage, cinquefoil), bloodletting on the hand or arm, a wrist plaster applied before the paroxysm, an explanation of why fevers keep their hourly periodicity and the prognostic sign of lip/nose blisters, followed by a detailed curative regimen for tertian fever using emetics, jalap/scammony/antimony purgatives, and spirit of vitriol potions.

Page 183 (folio verso) contains Early New High German and Latin medical recipes for external and internal fever remedies ('Etliche Euserliche mittel Wider das fieber'), including foot plasters, sympathetic/magical remedies using a spider in a nutshell and plantain roots tied to the pulse or neck, cinquefoil leaves, celandine, ordinary fever drinks, St. Ambrose's fever potion, fever potions with blessed thistle and theriac water, and a series of fever powders and elderberry/celandine remedies. Illustrated with a pointing manicule in the upper left margin and a shaded ink-and-wash pitcher/jug beside the ordinary fever drink.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration 1 (Canvas 154)** (`#xywh=850,500,2185,1800`): A pointing hand (manicule) with a dark cuff drawn in ink and wash in the upper left column, pointing right toward the first fever plaster recipe.

**Illustration 2 (Canvas 154)** (`#xywh=850,2300,2185,1800`): A shaded ink-and-wash drawing of a round-bellied pitcher/jug with a handle and a small loaf or stone beside it, placed to the left of the rubric 'in den fieber Solle das ordinari Trankh sein volgents'.

Page 184 (folio recto) presents recipes for ordinary fever drinks ('Waßer für das ordinari Trankh in Jeden fieber'), cooling drinks for feverish patients and thirst, a water substitute for wine, followed by a treatise on double tertian and continuous fevers ('Volgt Weider Von den Dopleten 3 taglichen auch Continuierlichen fiebern') with electuaries, laxative chicory vinegar, and purging/post-purging regimens. Illustrated with a shaded ink-and-wash pitcher/jug at the top of the left column.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration 1 (Canvas 155)** (`#xywh=350,500,2373,1800`): A small shaded ink-and-wash drawing of a round-bellied jug/pitcher with a handle in the upper left margin beside the rubric 'Waßer für das ordinari Trankh in Jeden fieber'.

Page 185 (folio verso) continues with fever remedies in full-width lines across the upper two-thirds, covering quotidian, tertian, and stomach fevers (including roasted nutmeg, quenched iron in wine, asarabacca, coriander in a soft egg, and a sympathetic dough-and-dog remedy for children). The lower third features a framed colored illustration on the left of a wrapped elderly/sickly person leaning on a staff beside a door, captioned with critical and decretory days, paired on the right with a treatise explaining 'Dies Critici' and 'Dies Decretorii' (critical and decretory days in severe fevers, highlighting day 7 as the most dangerous).

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**dies Critici. 7. 14. 21. 27. / dies Decretorej. 4. 9. 14. 17. 21. 23. 27.** (`#xywh=850,500,2201,1800`): A framed colored ink-and-wash illustration in the lower left showing an elderly or sickly figure wearing a white headwrap, dark cloak with a yellow collar, and long reddish-brown skirt, leaning on a walking stick indoors beside a wooden door.

Continuation of fever treatment (cooling broth, mild laxative, leeches to the hemorrhoidal vein, cupping glasses, and senna/rhubarb infusion), followed by sections on symptoms of double continuous tertian fever ('febre Terzana dopio Continoe'), its cure ('Chur') including bloodletting, clysters, boluses, and emetics, and a section on sweating ('Von Schwizen in disen fieber').

Two-column page continuing remedies for excessive sweating (astringent oils, cooling air), followed by sections on continual vomiting ('Von Continuierlichen Bröchen') with recipes using quince juice, corals, and oxymel, a recipe section ('So braucht Volgente Mitel') for phlegm and melancholy vomiting, and a section on insomnia in fever ('Von lohrnen Schlaff, V über flisiges Wachen in fieber') with cooling diets, melon milk, and soporific foot-baths.

Two-column page continuing external and internal soporific remedies (opium/saffron ointment, poppy syrup, Philonium Romanum, Trifera magna), followed by a section on lethargy/sleeping sickness in fever ('Schlaff Sucht. in fieber') with clysters, suppositories ('Zäpfl.'), tickling the nose, shaving the head, and a colored drawing of a human head showing the coronal suture ('Commissura Coronale') for topical/cautery application, plus a precious syrup recipe.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration of the coronal suture on the head (adjacent to 'Volgenter Sÿrup ist sehr khöstlich')** (`#xywh=350,500,2200,1800`): Pen-and-ink and watercolor wash drawing of a human head tilted slightly forward, with brown curly hair, downcast eyes, nose, and mouth. Red lines mark a horizontal band around the forehead/temples intersecting a vertical line along the sagittal suture at a small red circle on the coronal suture ('Commissura Coronale'), illustrating the site of application referenced in the text above.

Treatise on petechiae (spotted fever), classifying red, white/violet, and yellow/black spots by severity and prognosis, accompanied by a watercolor illustration of a spotted patient holding a rosary in bed attended by a female caregiver, followed by purgative, blistering, bezoar, Armenian bole, and cooling remedies, including treatments for pregnant women.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration of a patient with petechiae in bed** (`#xywh=350,500,2360,1800`): Framed rectangular watercolor showing a bearded male patient propped up on white pillows in a wooden bed under a white sheet, bare-chested with red petechial spots on his torso and arms, wearing a red headband and holding a long black-and-gold rosary; to the right stands a female attendant in a purplish-pink dress and dark cap holding a shallow brown basin, with a table bearing a bowl of red fruit in the background.

Continuation of the petechial drink recipe, followed by sections on Febris Epiala (coldness predominating over heat), Febris Lipyria (internal burning with external coldness, symptoms, and cooling/bleeding treatment), and Febris Ardens (burning fever from yellow bile, mortal symptoms, and cooling/purgative cures).

Treatise on Febris Quartana (four-day fever), attributed to putrid melancholic bile and tough phlegm; the author criticizes slow conventional methods and presents his own successful multi-stage cure consisting of purgative powders, drinks, or electuaries, digestive pills, and an herbal broth.

Page 195 (verso) of Wellcome Collection MS.990 contains early modern German and Latin medical recipes for treating quartan and tertian fevers. The left column presents a complex electuary ('Die Lattwerung mach also') incorporating aromatic roots, herbs, hartshorn, coral, seeds, honey, and Peruvian bark (cinchona), followed by detailed German dosing and regimen instructions. The right column continues the regimen, warning against overindulgence after recovery, and adds four further fever remedies ('Volgen noch andere Mitl fir das 4 tägliche fieber', two entries titled 'Ein Anders', and 'Arcana fir das 4 tägliche vnd 3 tägliche fieber') using mithridatium, Peruvian bark, arcanum duplicatum, antimony, alchemical salts, laudanum, and herbal infusions. Two ink manicules appear on the page (one in the left column beside 'hirundinaria. Scorzonera. āā ℥j.' and one beneath the final red heading in the right column).

A 17th-century German and Latin medical recipe collection (Wellcome Collection MS.990, p. 396) arranged in two columns, containing remedies and purgative potions for quartan and continuous fevers, including herbal decoctions, emollient poultices for splenic pain, gentian, rose water, tobacco water, peppercorns, and a foot cataplasm.

Folio 97 verso, titled 'Von den Ungewissen fieber, oder Ungewissen kranckheit' (Of the uncertain fever, or uncertain illness), attributes epidemic or 'uncertain' fevers to divine punishment and miasmatic corruption of the air caused by unfavorable celestial constellations and planetary aspects. A large central watercolor illustration depicts a bare-chested patient sitting up in bed attended by a physician gesturing toward medicines and a crucifix on a table, while a weeping woman stands in the doorway on the left. The text below describes how poisoned air and crops transmit toxins into the body, producing diverse symptoms such as intense heat, inflammation, severe headache, unquenchable thirst, diarrhea, and loss of senses/appetite.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Bedside scene of a fever patient, physician, and grieving woman** (`#xywh=850,500,2185,1800`): A central watercolor illustration showing a bare-chested patient with wavy brown hair sitting propped up on white pillows in a wooden bed under a white sheet and mottled rose-red coverlet. To the right, a physician in a black skullcap, white collar, and fur-trimmed robe rests his right hand on the patient's shoulder while pointing with his left toward a wooden table beneath a four-paned window; on the table stand a small crucifix, apothecary jars and flasks (containing yellow and pink liquids), and a bowl with a spoon. On the far left, a woman in a red bodice and white skirt stands in an open doorway, holding a cloth to her face in grief.

A folio from a late 17th-century German medical manuscript (Wellcome MS.990, p. 398) discussing contagious fevers ('Contagios oder anfengig'). The text describes how pestilential poisons enter the body through air, food, drink, breath, stench, or fear, attacking the heart and brain. It provides preventive measures including fumigation with juniper wood, masterwort, and lovage, along with purgation, bloodletting, and several compound recipes (an electuary with theriac, Armenian bole, and alkermes; pills with myrrh, gum ammoniac, and aloes; and a 'famous poison powder' of valerian, swallowwort, polypody, lovage, angelica, and herb Paris). The final section addresses the cure of the fever, noting its severity as a divine punishment requiring repentance before natural remedies, and warning physicians that deceptive pulses and urine signs can mask the illness.

Folio 99 verso of Wellcome Collection MS.990 (c. 1675) continues a treatise on pestilential fever and its treatment. The left column outlines the fivefold (headed '4 weg') therapeutic regimen—air correction, vomitives, purgation via the bowels, sweating, and tempering of heat and cold—followed by diagnostic signs of acute thirst, precordial oppression, and shivering, and introduces a protective fumigation ('Rauch') accompanied by an illustration of a smoking censer. The right column provides the compound fumigation recipe (including olibanum, amber, myrrh, mastic, asa foetida, hartshorn, angelica, pimpernel, and spun hemp, silk, gold, and silver threads) and a section on therapeutic vomiting ('Yber brechen in disen fieber') illustrated by a man vomiting into a tub, recommending mild emetics such as linseed, walnut, or bitter almond oil, hazelwort with oxymel, and a feather dipped in scorpion oil.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Fumigation censer (bottom left)** (`#xywh=850,500,2199,1800`): A footed chalice-like censer or brazier resting on a yellow base, filled with glowing red-orange coals and herbs, with grey smoke billowing upward and a small ladle or pestle resting against the left side.

**Man vomiting into a tub (middle right)** (`#xywh=850,2300,2199,1800`): A bearded man in a grey tunic leaning forward over a round, banded wooden or ceramic tub, vomiting a stream of yellow-red bilious matter into the vessel while holding its rim.

Folio 208r of Wellcome MS.990 presents two columns of 17th-century German and Latin medical recipes and therapeutic instructions. The left column opens with a secret arcanum ('Ein schönes Arcana') prepared by distilling bryony root, cyclamen root, and white hellebore in water, administered in Malmsey wine via a small glass pipette (accompanied by an inline triangular symbol/sketch of the glass tip) to purge contagious poisons from the stomach, followed by a section attributed to 'H. Rönötten' on removing the cause of the illness through purgation, clysters, bloodletting, and especially sweating. The right column discusses sweating as a sure remedy for this and other fevers, warning against overheating ingredients (brandy, pepper, pellitory, castoreum, camphor, sulfur), debating whether camphor cools or heats, and providing several sudorific recipes (angelica root with theriac, elecampane in red wine, lovage root with wine vinegar, rue juice with theriac) as well as external warming methods using vinegar-moistened bricks, hot water flasks, and a vinegar-and-theriac compress applied over the navel.

Page 201 (verso) in two columns. The upper left continues a regimen on managing sweat and preventing sleep in poisoned or feverish patients (including heart-strengthening cordials). The main section 'Vom Aderlasen' (Of Bloodletting) argues against bloodletting in this continuous fever because it weakens the body's moisture and drives heat toward the heart, brain, chest, or kidneys, followed by a red rubric noting that experience shows all who died had been bled. The right column concludes with remarks on aiding natural purgation (vomiting, suppositories, or laxative foods).

Page 202 (recto) in two columns. Continues general remarks on fever heat, then presents 'Von der Hiz, und dero Küellung' (Of Heat and its Cooling), detailing cooling foods, waters, syrups (rose, violet, lemon, pomegranate, mulberry, elderberry, citron), and warning against applying cold poultices directly to the heart or stomach. The right column adds lukewarm ointments, cooling lotions (rosewater, nightshade, salt, rue), and introduces 'Von Allerley Zue fäll dises fiebers, als erstlich von der Tobsucht und haubt Wehe' (Of All Kinds of Symptoms of this Fever, Firstly Frenzy and Headache).

Page 203 (verso), written in a single full-page column. Continues distinguishing the symptoms of hot/bilious headache and lethargy, then presents 'Von den hitzigen bösenden Kopff Wehe' (Of the Hot Malignant Headache) with recipes for rosewater, salt, Armenian bole, barley milk, and—if delirium ensues—applying a freshly split black hen or warm calf/lamb lung to the shaved head. Concludes with 'Von khalten Schläfferigen Wehe tage des Haubts' (Of Cold Lethargic Headache) and a spiced vinegar decoction (angelica, masterwort, zedoary, tormentil, dittany, red roses, marjoram, lavender).

Page 204 (recto) of Wellcome MS.990, arranged in two columns, continues remedies for sleeping sickness (Schlafsucht) including external plasters, vinegar-boiled herbs, and brain-raging treatments; followed by a major red-ink heading 'Von den Wirmen in diser khranckheit' (Of the worms in this sickness) detailing symptoms of parasitic worms, anthelmintic powders (rhubarb, aloe, myrrh, carline thistle, euphorbium, hartshorn, dittany, corallina), and a second major red-ink heading 'Von den Schwaissen' (Of the sweats) introducing critical vs. non-critical sweats.

Page 205 (verso), arranged in two columns, continues the treatise on sweats ('Von den Schwaissen'), distinguishing two types: non-decretory cold/clammy sweats (with warnings against featherbeds, instructions to prevent sleep by applying red/rose vinegar with lavender or rosewater to the nose and pulses) and critical sweats ('sudores critici') on the 3rd, 5th, or 7th day (to be wiped with warm cloths and checked with quince or myrtle oil if excessive). In the lower right column, a major red-ink heading 'Von Vergicht, Krampf, Omachten und sewer gliedrn' introduces convulsions, cramps, fainting, and heavy limbs.

Page 206 (recto), written in a single full-page column, concludes the chapter on convulsions and cramps with instructions to bind the patient with soft cloths, revive them with amber smoke, frankincense, angelica, and rub the limbs with cooling or warming oils (rose, violet, goose/duck fat vs. castoreum, chamomile, fox fat). A major red-ink heading 'Von Ver Liehrung Und Widerbringung der Khräfften' (Of the Loss and Restoration of Strengths) then discusses the three spirits (animalis, vitalis, naturalis) and prescribes nourishing broths, capon, chicken, veal, doves, alkermes, rosewater, lemon/citron juice, and aromatics.

Continuation of a treatise on acute/continuous fevers, covering cooling remedies for a heated liver, sudden swoonings (Von Jächlingen omachten) from cold, heat, or bleeding, heart palpitations (Von Gertz khlopffen), facial signs of impending death (Hippocratic facies), and cordial heart-poultices and smelling-bags (Volgen Von den herz Söckhsen).

Continuation of cordial poultice and aqua vitae recipes for swooning, followed by a new illustrated section on secondary facial, ear, gum, and cheek symptoms (Von andern Zuefällen als fallen sind an den ohren am Wang, augen vnd Zanfleisch vnd geschwulst des angesichts), featuring a watercolor bust portrait of a youth with a red cheek swelling, and remedies for cheek/jaw swellings, toothache, and ear discharge/deafness.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Portrait of a youth with a cheek swelling** (`#xywh=850,500,2344,1800`): Framed watercolor bust portrait in the upper-middle left column depicting a young man with dark curly hair facing forward, showing a prominent, rounded, inflamed red swelling on his left cheek (malar/parotid region), illustrating the section on facial, ear, and cheek swellings.

Illustrated medical treatise sections covering Eye Pains (Augen schmerzen), with recipes for eye-drops and poultices; Nosebleeds (Von Nasen Fluetten), noting critical-day bleeding vs. dangerous hemorrhage; and Quinsy, Mouth, Tonsil, and Throat Ulcers (Von der Brein. Mundt Mandel vnd Hals geschwer), with gargle recipes.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Human Eye** (`#xywh=350,500,2219,1800`): Square framed watercolor illustration in the top-left corner depicting a single human eye with brown iris and eyelids, accompanying the section 'Augen schmerzen' (Eye Pains).

**Youth with Nosebleed** (`#xywh=350,2300,2219,1800`): Framed watercolor illustration in the bottom-left corner depicting a young man in profile wearing a yellow-brown garment, leaning forward with blood streaming from his nose into a small bowl held beneath his chin, accompanying the section 'Von Nasen. Fluetten' (Of Nosebleeds).

Continuation of remedies for dry tongue and mouth in fever (including psyllium/tragacanth mucilage, fresh butter/onion juice in rose vinegar, and houseleek with purified saltpetre/nitre), followed by a new section 'Von der Particular Angina in disen fieber' describing malignant/pestilential angina (quinsy) with erythema around the neck and chest, its rapid 24-hour to 7-day course, symptoms, and caution against bloodletting or purging except to protect the principal organs.

Two-column page containing two major sections: 'Von durch Brechen' (on diarrhoea/fluxes and vomiting caused by ingested poison or corrupted air/fruit, distinguishing fatal black/bloody fluxes from critical evacuations, followed by stomach-strengthening recipes using tormentil, ginger, cinnamon, paradise wood, mace, aristolochia, calamus, galangal, zedoary, and mastic) and 'Von Mißgeburdt in disem fieber' (on miscarriage and premature birth in fever, advising cautious purging and bloodletting between the 4th and 7th months using mild laxatives like manna and cassia).

Page 213 discusses dangerous blood fluxes and symptoms during malignant fevers in pregnant women, advising caution and moderation in bloodletting (phlebotomy) to preserve the fetus. It provides compound remedies, including a theriac electuary, external salves, and herbal decoctions (scolopendrium, hedera terrestris, ribwort plantain) to prevent miscarriage, as well as powders (white dittany, nigella, unicorn horn, hazel mistletoe) to aid difficult childbirth and expel a dead fetus or afterbirth. At the bottom, a new section begins under a red rubric concerning uterine flux (symbolized by ☿) in this fever.

Page 214 concludes the section on excessive uterine bleeding during fever, recommending ligatures on the fingers, cupping glasses on the spleen and liver, and an electuary of rose sugar, blackthorn root, terra sigillata, and red rose juice. A major red rubric then introduces 'Spots, Flea-like Pustules, Petechiae, and Eruptions in this Fever,' accompanied by a colored inset illustration of a seated nude youth covered in red spots. The text distinguishes contagious fever spots caused by poisoned air from children's smallpox/measles ('Durchschlächten'), detailing their colors and prognostic significance.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Zu der 11 sagen** (`#xywh=350,500,2295,1800`): Colored ink and watercolor illustration on the left side of the page showing a nude youth wearing a red cap, seated on a rectangular block in an outdoor landscape, with red spots and pustules (petechiae/pox) distributed across his chest, arms, legs, and face.

Page 215, laid out in two columns, presents the treatment for fever pustules, petechiae, and smallpox-like eruptions. The left column warns against chilling the patient or overheating them with excessive bedclothes, and gives two detailed Latin apothecary recipes: a precious-stone cordial powder (bezoardic/cordial powder with pearls, corals, bole, ivory, dittany, camphor, zedoary, saffron, and behen) and a gilded electuary (conserve of roses, borage, bugloss, theriac, mithridate, gold leaf, and citron syrup). The right column offers topical and supportive remedies: lentil and fig waters with vinegar, white rose oil and Solomon's seal for facial skin, juniper-quince salves for ulcerating pustules, and woman's milk, rose honey, or pomegranate gargles for pustules in the mouth, eyes, nose, and throat.

Treatise on common hot and malignant fevers ('Von den Gemeinen Hizigen fieber'), describing their humoral causes (yellow bile, poisonous humors entering the blood), pulse characteristics (using Latin sphygmological terms such as intercidentes, vermiculantes, caprizantes, and formicantes), diagnostic signs, and therapeutic goals centered on early emetics, clysters, and diaphoretic (sweat-inducing) prescriptions using hartshorn, diaphoretic antimony, cinnabar of antimony, theriac, and herbal waters. No illustrations.

Continuation of fever therapeutics: diaphoretic and cordial prescriptions (including volatile salt of hartshorn, occidental and oriental bezoar, pearls, corals, and juleps), cautions against late bloodletting and purging, rules for maintaining gentle warmth and sweat, and management of critical signs (buboes, spots, nosebleeds, diarrhea, and relapse prevention). Begins a new major section 'Von Underschiedlichen Zuefälen So sich bey den hizigen fieber begeben' ('Of Various Symptoms Occurring in Hot Fevers'), starting with severe headache remedies. No illustrations.

Continuation of symptom-specific remedies for hot fevers in a full-page layout: treatments for lethargy/sleeping sickness ('Schlaffsucht'), constant wakefulness/insomnia ('Stetes Wachen', warning against internal opium), poultices for the heart, pulse, and soles of the feet, delirium, the patient's ordinary hartshorn drink, pleurisy/lung inflammation with a pectoral decoction, hiccups ('Schlugutzen') and nausea, and excessive/painful urination. No illustrations.

Two-column medical manuscript page (p. 220, recto) featuring an ink-and-wash bust portrait of a bearded man in a brown habit in the upper-left corner, followed by a treatise on hectic or consumptive fever ('Von der hectica oder dörrsichtigen fieber'), detailing its three degrees, causes, prognosis, diet, and internal remedies.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Portrait of a bearded man** (`#xywh=350,500,2329,1800`): Ink and wash bust portrait in the upper-left corner of the left column, depicting a bearded man with a tonsure or skullcap wearing a brown habit or robe, framed within a red-ruled border.

Single-column medical manuscript page (p. 221, verso) containing six therapeutic recipes for consumptive patients ('die dörrsichtigen'), including four medicinal baths (using hazelnut ash lye, goat's milk, sheep's and calves' feet, mallows, and herbs) and two nourishing, healing distilled waters and jellies.

Remedies for hectic fever (hectica) and wasting/consumption (abnemen), followed by a colored anatomical illustration of a man pulling open his chest to reveal the heart and lungs, and an introductory treatise on pulmonary phthisis (Lungelsucht / Tisisie), its contagion, dietary regimen, and initial honey-based electuary.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration 1 (Canvas 193)** (`#xywh=350,500,2336,1800`): Colored ink and wash anatomical illustration in the lower left column depicting a bare-chested man wearing a yellow-ochre cap with brown trim, using both hands to pull open a diamond-shaped incision in his chest, exposing the red heart, lungs, and ribcage.

Continuation of recipes for lung-sickness and consumption (Lungelsucht / Dörrsucht), including electuaries with marshmallow and elecampane, a secretum of ground ivy juice and flowers of tin/sulphur, pectoral powders, snail broth, a cooling syrup for hemoptysis, cynoglossa pills, a goat's milk gruel, and a chest and lung powder.

Folio 226v continues a treatise on pulmonary consumption (Lungensucht / phthisis), detailing prognostic signs (purulent sputum, night sweats, urine sediment, hair loss, diarrhea, and angina) and presenting several compound remedies including Balsam of Sulfur, Tincture of Tin/Jupiter, Saffron Tincture, Venetian turpentine pills, lozenges to correct acrimony, and a decoction/water for consumptive patients.

Folio 227r is laid out in two columns. The left column continues the distilled pulmonary water recipe from f. 226v, adds a marshmallow-iris julep, warns against strong purgatives for consumptives (offering a mild laxative drink instead), and gives a laudanum/cynoglossum pill remedy for children's whooping cough. The right column concludes the pill recipe and presents a 'wonderful secretum' (aloes compress on the stomach), a 'precious lung drink' of herbs and raisins, 'Another' calf's-lung distillation, and a gold-leaf secretum for consumption.

Folio 228v opens the chapter 'Von Bluet speiben' (On Spitting of Blood / Hemoptysis) in two columns. The upper-left features a colored watercolor illustration of a woman vomiting/spitting blood into a bowl. The left column explains the causes, diagnostic distinctions (lung vs. chest vs. stomach vs. head bleeding), and prognosis of hemoptysis. The right column discusses fever-related risks, bloodletting (arm, hand, foot, and leeches to the hemorrhoidal vein), dietary regimen, and three remedies: turpentine/Indian balsam pills with China/sarsaparilla decoction, a 'wonderful electuary' of henbane, poppy, terra sigillata, and red coral, and a 'special remedy' of crab ashes dissolved in vinegar.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration above 'Von Bluet speiben' (f. 228v, upper left)** (`#xywh=850,500,2223,1800`): Colored ink and watercolor illustration depicting a woman in 17th-century attire (headscarf/cap with red ribbons, yellow bodice over a white chemise, red skirt) leaning forward and holding a dark ceramic bowl into which she is spitting/vomiting a stream of bright red blood.

A 17th-century German and Latin medical manuscript page (folio 229r) containing remedies for haemorrhage and haemoptysis (spitting of blood). The left column presents several astringent powders, a secret remedy using eggshell membrane and plantain water, boluses, and a 'wonderful effect' recipe using mouse or rat dung. The right column continues with purgative/astringent instructions using rhubarb, oxymel, and theriac, followed by a decoction for spitting of blood, a chemical preparation of 'Balsam ♃' (balsam of sulphur/tin with turpentine), and a final section on treating haemoptysis with rhubarb, linden charcoal, and blessed thistle water.

Folio 230 verso from Wellcome Collection MS.990 (c. 1675), containing medical notes and recipes in Early New High German with Latin pharmaceutical terminology. The left column concludes a remedy for disordered blood (recommending rhubarb to draw water from the blood), followed by an ink-and-watercolor illustration of a patient inhaling medicinal vapors beneath a linen tent over a brazier. Below the illustration, a section titled 'Fluß Chatar' defines catarrh as phlegm and moisture rising from the stomach, spleen, liver, or womb into the head like vapors in an alembic, listing resulting ailments (apoplexy, abscesses, ear/eye/tooth pain, angina, suffocative catarrh, gout, sciatica). The right column continues the typology of cold and hot catarrhs, prescribes universal purges (emetics, Hauptpillen, syrups of betony, stoechas, calendula, sage, rosemary, violets, chicory), and provides two recipes in red-headed sections: a fumigation ('Volgenter Rauch Ist Köstlich') with white amber, mastic, cloves, and masterwort, and a medicated head fomentation/cap ('Bäthe auf das haubt für Catar... f. Scuffia') with hartshorn, barley, bran, marjoram, betony, red roses, Arabian stoechas, camel's hay, fennel, sweet flag, and mastic.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Fluß Chatar** (`#xywh=850,500,2215,1800`): Watercolor and ink illustration of a figure wearing a white linen cloth draped like a tent over the head and shoulders, wearing a red bodice and white sleeves, leaning over an ochre table to inhale vapors rising from a dark footed brazier or chafing dish filled with glowing coals and medicinal substances.

Folio 231 recto from Wellcome MS.990 (c. 1675) presents German and Latin medical recipes and clinical commentary in two columns. The left column contains four fumigation (Rauch) recipes for hot and cold catarrhs and fluxes of the head, followed by an electuary and mutton-broth remedy for prolonged coughing and wheezing, and begins a section on hot catarrh (Von den Hitzigen Catarrn). The right column continues the treatment of hot catarrh—discussing bloodletting, a rhubarb-tamarind purgative, laudanum opiatum, and chest syrups (including coltsfoot), as well as hoarseness—before introducing a new major section on coughing (Von dem Huesten), detailing its physiology, causes (phlegm from the head, vapors from liver, stomach, spleen, or womb, and lung ulcers), and therapeutic cautions.

Continuation of cough remedies including elecampane preparations, hot-cough electuaries, children's cough remedies, and external chest salves, followed by a section on great thirst ('Von Großen Durst') accompanied by a watercolor illustration of a woman drinking from a pitcher, and cooling waters/juleps for thirst.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Von Großen Durst.** (`#xywh=850,500,2221,1800`): Ink and watercolor illustration of a woman in profile facing left, wearing a red bodice with white sleeves and a yellow-trimmed headdress, holding a large grey pewter or silver pitcher to her mouth with both hands to drink, standing on a green ground.

Treatise on diseases of the heart ('Von kranckheit des Herzens') with an anatomical heart illustration, detailing the causes and cure of cardiac weakness (including a recipe for distilled bull's-heart broth), followed by numerous recipes for heart-strengthening drinks, boluses, cordial pills, heart compresses/poultices, and heart-strengthening salves/sachets.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration 1 (Canvas 203)** (`#xywh=350,500,2337,1800`): Watercolor illustration of a red anatomical heart positioned above a rectangular ink-drawn frame at the top of the left column.

Continuation of heart-strengthening remedies, including compresses, electuaries, heart salves, and cordials with precious stones and magisteries. The lower half introduces a section on heart palpitation and trembling ('Von dem Herz klopffen vnd Zitern') beside a large watercolor illustration of a horizontal anatomical heart, followed by remedies against palpitations.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration 1 (Canvas 204)** (`#xywh=850,500,2216,1800`): Large watercolor illustration of an anatomical heart oriented horizontally with its apex pointing left, located in the lower-left quadrant beside the treatise on heart palpitation.

Folio 235r (two columns) continues a section on syncope/fainting and cardiac weakness in the left column, prescribing external applications, bloodletting, internal cordials, two heart ointments ('Xolgendes Sälbel'), and cordial emulsions ('Emulsian Cordial'). The right column opens with a recipe for precious heart lozenges ('Andere Khöstliche Hertz Zeltlen') followed by a clinical treatise on 'Prust Apostem' (thoracic aposteme/empyema), detailing its symptoms, differential diagnosis, causes, and prognosis.

Folio 236v (two columns) continues the prognosis and treatment of breast aposteme/empyema. The left column provides emollient poultices and plasters, a pectoral decoction ('Prust Tranckh'), and a linctus ('Zum Leckhen Dis Xolgendes'). The right column describes surgical thoracentesis (incising between the third and fourth ribs to drain pus gradually), a supplementary linseed/sugar remedy, and concludes with a section on 'Prust Wassersucht' (hydrothorax / dropsy of the breast).

Folio 237r (two columns) features a large hand-colored sickbed illustration at the top of the left column, followed by a treatise 'Von den Schmerzlichen Seiden Stechen' (Of the Painful Side-Stitches / Pleurisy). The text defines true pleurisy (pleuritis exquisita / legitima) as an inflammation of the pleura and lists its five cardinal symptoms. The right column continues the symptoms, prognostic signs (including conversion to empyema after 14 days and the critical 7th day), and introduces false pleurisy ('Das falsche Seiden stich Spuria oder Bastärdt').

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration 1 (Canvas 207)** (`#xywh=350,500,2345,1800`): Hand-colored gouache/watercolor sickbed scene in the upper left column: a pale, bearded patient lies propped up in a wooden bed under white-and-blue-shaded sheets. A physician or attendant in a green coat stands beside the bed offering a red chalice/cup of medicine, while a woman in a red bodice and dark skirt looks in through an open doorway on the right. Below the scene is a blank rectangular cartouche framed in gold.

Medical treatise on pleurisy (Seitenstechen), discussing humoral causes (wind, bile, phlegm, melancholy), diagnostic signs from expectoration and pulse/fever, critical days (4th, 7th, and 9th), and therapeutic regimens including clysters, bloodletting on the affected side, cupping, gentle laxatives (cassia, manna), internal warming oils, and external poultices and fomentations.

Further recipes for pleurisy and apostemes, organized by time and day of illness: bedtime juices (licorice, maidenhair, violet julep, red poppy), oriental bezoar, fomentations and pectoral ointments for days 3–4 to mature and break the aposteme, safe chamomile-and-sugar-candy draughts for day 4, sweet almond oil remedies, and soothing plasters/cataplasms with marshmallow, cabbage leaves, and fenugreek.

Page 236 (recto) begins with a powder recipe for pleurisy (Seiden Stöchen), followed by a painted profile portrait of a bearded man above a blank cartouche. Below the illustration, a new section on asthma (Asthma, oder Engbrüstigkeit) discusses its humoral causes, symptoms, diagnostic distinction between cold and heat, and remedies including vesicatories, cupping, fox-lung powder, Elixir proprietatis, a conserve, and a tincture.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Blank cartouche beneath profile portrait of a man** (`#xywh=350,500,2327,1800`): Watercolour and ink profile portrait facing left of a man with curly brown hair, a dark upturned moustache, and a small chin beard, set against a pale blue wash above an empty rectangular cartouche.

Page 237 (verso) continues the treatise on asthma with recipes for currant-and-ginger decoction, lozenges (troches), conserves, pills of woodlice and benzoin, balsam of benzoin, laudanum opiatum, and antimonial balsam. It also includes clinical notes on whether vomiting and sweating are advisable in asthma, concluding with a recipe for a sacratum.

Page 238 (recto) concludes the sacratum recipe and adds pills and a mead decoction for clearing phlegm, followed by a short treatise on dropsy of the chest (hydrothorax / brust Waßer sucht). The right column features a watercolour illustration of a man lying supine in a landscape, followed by emergency resuscitation instructions for suffocation from smoke, drowning, or hanging.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Man lying prostrate in a landscape** (`#xywh=350,500,2324,1800`): Watercolour and ink illustration showing a bearded man in a red coat/tunic, dark breeches, and black shoes lying supine on grassy green ground with a winding path and dark green trees/bushes in the background.
