Page 239 (verso) opens the section on diseases of the stomach ('Von des Magen Kranckheiten'). At the top of the left column is a red-wash anatomical illustration of the stomach above an empty cartouche. The text discusses the humoral causes of stomach ailments (viscous phlegm, bile, melancholy, heat, and cold), the physiological role of the pylorus and stomach ferment in digestion, relaxation of the pylorus leading to lientery/diarrhea, remedies including hard egg yolks, nutmeg, and a closing powder, and symptoms of bilious heat versus cold phlegmatic matter in the stomach.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration 1 (Canvas 214)** (`#xywh=850,500,2234,1800`): Red-wash anatomical illustration of the human stomach at the top of the left column, showing the esophagus entering from the upper right and the duodenum/pylorus curving to the upper left, set above a blank yellow-bordered cartouche.

Page 240 (recto) continues the discussion of stomach ailments, addressing cold phlegmatic accumulation, sympathetic illness from the liver, dietary excesses, and the difficulty of curing chronic cold stomach conditions. It recommends emetics (blessed water, English salt, Tartarum Emeticum) followed by a herbal decoction of mint, betony, calamus, angelica, and mastic. The second half of the page discusses the causes of stomach weakness ('Die Schwachheit des Magen khumbt Von'), particularly overeating and excessive purging.

Page 241 (verso) presents treatments for weakness of the stomach ('Cur in Schwacheit des Magn'), beginning with internal preparatory syrups (syrup of violets and roses with lentisk or tamarind), purgative pills of rhubarb and aloes, and a cooling decoction for the hot liver. It then gives multiple external recipes: fomentations ('Fumonda') with aromatic herbs in red wine or sour water, strengthening plasters with labdanum, aloes, and expressed nutmeg oil, three variations of herbal stomach bags ('Magn Säckhel'), and a warming stomach ointment ('Salbe') for a cold, weak stomach.

Page 242 (recto) contains a collection of German and Latin pharmaceutical recipes for stomach complaints, including cerates, plasters (such as the 'Geisterliche Magen-Pflaster'), elixirs, electuaries (Lattwerung), a blessed thistle extract, an alchemical/bread-based stomach extract, and the beginning of a beef elixir.

Page 243 (verso) continues the recipe for the beef elixir, followed by recipes for a spiced wine, a stomach balsam, and a tincture of aloes and myrrh. The second half of the page transitions to medical theory regarding the stomach's central role in bodily health, chlorosis, vomiting, and lists penetrating aromatic herbs versus acid-tempering earths and salts.

Page 244 (recto) features a colored illustration at the top of the left column depicting a man vomiting into a basin held by a woman, with a pig or dog behind him. Below and in the right column is a clinical treatise on vomiting ('Von über bröchen des Magens'), detailing prognostic signs, contraindications (melancholics, children), causes (worms, bitter bile, phlegm, nervous irritation), and treatments using Tartarum Emeticum, Laudanum opiatum, and quince juice.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration of a vomiting patient** (`#xywh=350,500,2329,1800`): A colored pen-and-ink and watercolor illustration at the top of the left column. A woman in a green bodice and red skirt holds a basin while a man in a yellow doublet and red breeches leans forward and vomits into it. An animal (a pig or dog) stands on the right near a grassy mound, with an empty olive-bordered banner beneath the scene.

Continuation of recipes for stilling vomiting (including laudanum opiatum, theriac, mithridate, confection of hyacinth, and sourdough plasters), followed by a recipe for great stomach pains, a precious electuary for spoiled/weak stomachs, a sourdough-and-theriac plaster for persistent vomiting, and the start of a treatise 'Von Kluxen oder auffstossen des Magens' (Of Hiccups or Belching of the Stomach). No illustrations.

Continuation and remedies for hiccups (including laudanum opiatum, mint juice, electuary of quinces, and elixir proprietatis), followed by a section 'Vom Soot oder Magen Brenen' (Of Heartburn or Stomach Burning) recommending Armenian bole, spodium, chalk, and Species Diacreta Mynsichti, and then 'Magen krallen. Magen Wehe. Cardialgia' (Stomach Cramps, Stomach Ache, Cardialgia) with its pathology and the start of its cure. No illustrations.

Continuation of the cure for cardialgia/stomach ache (chamomile broth with laudanum opiatum, Electuary Diaphoenicon and Philonium Romanum, citron peel and galangal decoction, external wormwood/mastic/spikenard oils, and internal hartshorn/coral powder), followed by a treatise 'Von Verlohrnen apedit' (Of Lost Appetite) explaining the weakening of the stomach's ferment by cold phlegm, and 'Chur und hilff den Verlohrnen apedit Widerumb zu bringen' (Cure and Help to Bring Back Lost Appetite) prescribing purging pills with gum ammoniac, colocynth, and elixir proprietatis Paracelsi. No illustrations.

Continuation of remedies for loss of appetite (anorexia/apepsia) using herbal infusions, Mynsicht's Elixir Vitrioli, Paracelsus's Elixir Proprietatis, and stomachic powders; followed by a rubricated section on 'Fressucht' (bulimia / excessive appetite for food) with absorbent and astringent remedies (coral, pearls, crabs' eyes, burnt hartshorn, Armenian bole, and tobacco); and a rubricated section on 'Selzamer Apedit' (pica / strange appetite for earth, coals, chalk, etc.). No illustrations.

Conclusion of the section on strange appetite (pica), noting its occurrence in pregnant women and advising emetics, purgatives, and warming stomachics (Elixir Proprietatis, Electuarium Hiera Picra); followed by a major rubricated section on 'Geschwer oder Apostem des magens' (ulcers or abscesses of the stomach), detailing internal and external signs, causes (choleric blood, corrosive poisons like euphorbium and cantharides), grave prognosis, and a rubricated cure involving bloodletting, emetics for poison, cooling diet, clysters, and quince/bilberry juices. No illustrations.

Continuation of stomach ulcers/abscesses, describing suppuration, chronic ulcers, decoctions of China root and guaiacum (Franzosenholz), Armenian bole, Terra Sigillata, mastic oil, and Cyprian turpentine; followed by a rubricated section on 'Wan Grose Magen Schmerzen Verhanden' (severe stomach pains) with recipes using mastic, chamomile, nutmeg, elecampane, blessed thistle, sassafras, mint, and melissa; a cancelled/rubric-washed heading; and a rubricated section on 'Ein herliches Pflaster Vor große Schmerzen Und Schwachheit des Magen' (a splendid plaster for great pain and weakness of the stomach). No illustrations.

Medical recipes and materia medica in two columns, covering opiate/anodyne remedies for stomach pain, substances that strengthen the stomach and promote digestion (nutmeg, galangal, pepper, cinnamon), a stomach cerate (plaster), and a 'precious electuary' (Lattwerig) for strengthening the stomach, memory, and sight, and treating gout, vertigo, and phlegm.

Anatomical treatise in two columns with five watercolor illustrations: the portal veins (Pfordt Adern), umbilical veins (Nabel Adern) with bladder, the lungs (Von der Lungel) with trachea, the pericardium (Herz Heisel oder Pericartio), and the heart (Herz).

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Pfordt Adern** (`#xywh=350,500,2307,1800`): Watercolor illustration in upper-left margin showing a reddish-brown branching vascular tree representing the portal vein system.

**Nabel Adern** (`#xywh=350,2300,2307,1800`): Watercolor illustration in lower-left margin showing reddish-brown branching umbilical vessels descending to a pale oval bladder-like organ.

**Von der Lungel** (`#xywh=350,4100,2307,1800`): Watercolor illustration in upper-center showing the trachea (windpipe) descending into lobed pinkish-brown lungs.

**Herz Heisel oder Pericartio** (`#xywh=350,5900,2307,553`): Watercolor illustration in middle-center showing a pale conical pouch representing the pericardium.

**Herz** (`#xywh=350,7700,2307,-1247`): Watercolor illustration in lower-center showing a reddish-brown heart with yellowish-brown surface vessels/fat.

Anatomical treatise in two columns continuing the account of the heart, followed by sections on the heart chambers (Herz Khamer), heart valves (Thürlein des Herzen), diaphragm (Herz Bladt Diaphragma), liver (Leber), and gallbladder (Gall), accompanied by five watercolor anatomical illustrations.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Herz Khamer** (`#xywh=850,500,2238,1800`): Watercolor illustration in middle-left showing a reddish-brown cross-section of the heart with two V-shaped ventricular chambers.

**Thürlein des Herzen** (`#xywh=850,2300,2238,1800`): Watercolor illustration in lower-left showing a reddish-brown cross-section of the heart's two chambers and valve structures.

**Herz Bladt Diaphragma** (`#xywh=850,4100,2238,1800`): Watercolor illustration in upper-right showing a reddish-brown arched/domed diaphragm with small circular openings.

**Leber** (`#xywh=850,5900,2238,553`): Watercolor illustration in middle-right showing a reddish-brown liver with branching grey-white vessels and a small green gallbladder at the lower edge.

**Gall** (`#xywh=850,7700,2238,-1247`): Watercolor illustration in lower-right showing a yellowish-green elongated pear-shaped gallbladder and cystic duct.

Anatomical treatise in Early Modern German with Latin terminology covering the stomach (Magen), spleen (Miltz), pancreas (Ritzel), and mesentery (Gekröß / Mesenterio), accompanied by four colored ink-and-wash anatomical illustrations.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Magen (Stomach)** (`#xywh=350,500,2317,1800`): Greyish-brown ink-and-wash drawing of the stomach pouch showing the esophageal and pyloric openings.

**Miltz (Spleen)** (`#xywh=350,2300,2317,1800`): Brownish-grey bean-shaped anatomical drawing of the spleen with red branching splenic vessels entering at the hilum.

**Ritzel (Pancreas)** (`#xywh=350,4100,2317,1800`): Elongated tan-brown anatomical drawing of the pancreas with branching ducts or vessels extending downward.

**Gekröß / Mesenterio (Mesentery)** (`#xywh=350,5900,2317,553`): Circular anatomical illustration showing the grey-shaded coiled intestine surrounding a yellow-ochre mesentery with a dense network of branching red-brown mesenteric vessels and two main upper trunks.

Left column describes the six parts of the intestines (Därm), the omentum (das Nötz / omentum), and the peritoneum (Peritonea), each with an anatomical drawing. Right column concludes the peritoneum section and introduces a full-length colored illustration of a phlebotomy figure (bloodletting man / Aderlassmann) labeled with letters A–M.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Därm (Intestines)** (`#xywh=850,500,2231,1800`): Grey-shaded anatomical drawing of the coiled small intestine enclosed by the haustrated large intestine (colon).

**das Nötz / omentum (Omentum)** (`#xywh=850,2300,2231,1800`): Yellowish-tan pouch-like anatomical drawing of the greater omentum with fine branching red-brown blood vessels.

**Peritonea (Peritoneum)** (`#xywh=850,4100,2231,1800`): Grey-shaded shield-shaped anatomical drawing of the peritoneum showing the central umbilicus (navel) and branching vessels.

**Figur Und Verzaichnus der Bluet adern (Bloodletting Man / Aderlassmann)** (`#xywh=850,5900,2231,553`): Full-length colored ink-and-wash illustration of a standing male figure with long wavy brown hair and a white loincloth, standing on grassy ground, marked with capital letters (A, D, FE, H, L, M) indicating bloodletting veins.

### Left Column

Key (A–M) to the bloodletting figure on the facing verso (p. 257), followed by a comprehensive phlebotomy treatise detailing the principal veins of the upper and lower body (Cephalica, Basilica, Median, Axillaris, Salvatella, Ischiadica, Saphena, Poplitis, Stirn, and Näß adern) and the specific ailments treated by opening each vein.

Page 259 (verso) concludes a brief note on the lung vein and presents a detailed section 'Von Undscheid des Pluts' (On the Distinction of the Blood), explaining hematoscopy: how to judge blood consistency, viscosity, putrefaction, and the significance of differently colored foam (red, gold-yellow, white, blue) as indicators of the four humours. The right column continues with dietary and seasonal rules for bloodletting (wine vs. food, May/April vs. autumn, purging before venesection) and warnings against bleeding young children, pregnant or menstruating women, and postpartum patients.

Page 260 (recto) features a full-length red-ink anatomical illustration of the arterial system (numbered 114) in the left column, captioned 'Vena Pulsatilis Arteria', with text explaining that the artery originates in the left chamber of the heart and carries the most subtle vital spirits. The right column discusses the danger of accidentally striking an artery during bloodletting (especially near the liver vein), quantifies the pulse rate in healthy men (4,000 beats/hour) and choleric women (4,800 beats/hour), and introduces the section 'Von Greiffung der Puls' (On Feeling the Pulse), distinguishing pulse quantity (length, breadth, depth) and quality.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**114 / Vena Pulsatilis Arteria** (`#xywh=350,500,2315,1800`): Full-length frontal anatomical drawing in red ink depicting the human arterial tree, showing the aortic arch, carotid and brachial arteries, descending aorta with intercostal/visceral branches, and iliac/femoral arteries.

Page 261 (verso) continues the treatise on pulse diagnostics, cataloging the qualitative varieties of the pulse according to classical Galenic sphygmology: equal and unequal pulses, the recurrent pulse in the elderly, the intermittent/sawing ('verchlofne') pulse, the undulating wave-like ('wellende') pulse, the goat-leaping ('Caprisissa'), worm-like ('Wurmechtige / Vermicansa'), ant-like ('ameissige / formicansa') pulses—warning that the latter three portend death—as well as the trembling ('ziterte') pulse, the intercidens pulse in young healthy subjects, and weak pulses in malignant fevers.

Folio 262r continues a medical treatise on sphygmology (pulse diagnosis). It discusses the difficulty of recognizing the pulse, the proper comportment and technique of the physician when approaching the patient and taking the pulse (arm position, four-finger palpation, delicacy of hand, patient stillness and fasting, taking both hands, considering the patient's complexion and body heat), and variations of the pulse according to sex and age (men vs. women, elderly, youths, and children), concluding with an aphorism on the supreme importance of pulse knowledge.

Folio 263v continues the exposition on pulse diagnosis, analyzing the quality and quantity of the pulse, the prognostic value of the pulse in predicting the day and hour of a crisis, and the diagnostic meanings of weak, swift, slow, hasty, hard, and soft pulses. The lower right column introduces prognostic signs combining the pulse with urine, sweat, stool, and nosebleeds.

Folio 264r concludes the section on the pulse—discussing undulating (wellende), vermicular (worm-like), formicans (ant-like), trembling, and four-finger pulses—and transitions via a red rubricated heading ('Von den Zeichen des Urin') to uroscopy. The upper right column features a painted illustration of a physician holding up a glass urine flask (matula) for inspection, followed by observations on thick, turbid, white, and bloody urine in fevers.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Physician inspecting a urine flask (uroscopy)** (`#xywh=350,500,2332,1800`): Half-length ink-and-wash illustration in the upper half of the right column depicting a bearded physician facing left, dressed in a red sleeveless jerkin over yellow sleeves and a green patterned collar/undershirt. He holds up a glass matula (urine flask) filled with amber-yellow urine in his right hand to inspect it, while his left hand rests on his hip.

Conclusion of the uroscopy treatise (diagnosing kidney abscesses, bladder stones, bile/jaundice, blood spirits, cloud formations, and pregnancy from urine color and sediment) in the left column, paired in the right column with a full-length anatomical illustration of the venous system ('Figur der Vena Cava oder Bluet ader Samen') labeled with letters and alchemical symbols, followed by the opening lines on the liver as the origin of the veins.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Figur der Vena Caua. oder Bluet ader Samen** (`#xywh=850,500,2241,1800`): Full-body schematic anatomical drawing in red-brown ink depicting the venous system (Vena Cava) branching from the central trunk into the head, arms, torso, liver/kidneys, and legs. Specific veins and branches are keyed in black ink with uppercase and lowercase letters (A, B, C, D, E, I, P, R, S, T, V, W, X, a, b, e, g, h, i, k, n, o, q) and alchemical/astronomical symbols (⊙, ⊕, ⦶, ⦸) along the left leg, corresponding to the legend on p. 266.

Treatise on the venous system and the nature of blood (counting 368/365 veins, humoral qualities of blood across ages, sexes, and animal species, and emotional color changes), followed in the right column by a critique of traditional vein-specific bloodletting and a complete alphabetical and symbolic key (AA–DD, EE–ii, and four vein symbols) to the anatomical diagram on p. 265.

Illustrated treatise on bloodletting ('Von ader lasen. Wan Man Lasen Soll'), featuring a watercolor scene of a person having blood let into three bowls, a critique of superstitious bloodletting tables in favor of astronomical calendar aspects, and two tabular lists of favorable (red) and unfavorable (black) planetary conjunctions and aspects.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Von ader lasen. Wan Man Lasen Soll** (`#xywh=850,500,2234,1800`): Watercolor and ink illustration at the top of the left column depicting a figure with wavy brown hair and a grey-blue tunic seated behind a wooden table. Their right arm is extended to the left with a red ligature tied in a bow above the elbow; a thin stream of red blood arcs from the punctured vein into the middle of three small dark bowls containing blood on the table.

Page 268 introduces the six foundational constituents of the human body: the four elements (earth, fire, water, air) with their primary qualities, temperaments, bodily parts/limbs, the four humors (blood, choler, phlegm, melancholy) generated in the liver from chyle, and the three spirits (natural, vital, animal). An upper-left watercolor illustration depicts a nude human figure within a blue sphere flanked by the four alchemical elemental triangles.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Human figure surrounded by the four elemental symbols** (`#xywh=400,500,4621,1400`): Circular watercolor and ink illustration in the upper left column showing a standing nude human figure wearing a white loincloth inside a blue-shaded sphere, flanked at the four corners outside the circle by the alchemical triangles for Air (upper left), Fire (upper right), Water (lower left), and Earth (lower right).

Page 269 concludes the exposition of the three spirits (vital and animal) and the sixth constituent, the three faculties (animal, vital, and natural), noting age- and sex-based differences in bodily temperament. The right column opens a new section on the four humors of man, correlating blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and melancholy with the four elements and explaining the physiological roles of blood, yellow bile in the liver, and melancholy in the spleen.

Page 270 explains why yellow bile thins the blood and how black bile is distributed between the blood and the spleen, before introducing the sanguine (blood-rich) complexion. A bust portrait in the lower left column depicts a young sanguine person with a rosy complexion, followed by a detailed account of sanguine temperament, physical traits, pulse, urine, and the formation of blood from chyle.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

Page 271 continues the humoral treatise on blood (Sanguis), discussing its preparation from digestible food, its predominance in spring and in ages 25–35, and its purification into yellow bile and black/melancholic humor. The right column introduces unnatural humors derived from corrupted blood, followed by a color bust-length portrait of a choleric person and the opening of the section on the Choleric complexion.

Page 272 continues the account of the choleric temperament and bile (associated with the element of fire), lists the physical and psychological signs of excess bile, and discusses the unnatural sharp humor (subtypes of corrupted bile by color). The right column concludes with a color bust-length portrait of a phlegmatic person and introduces the Phlegmatic complexion.

Page 273 continues the description of the phlegmatic temperament, discusses phlegm (the watery humor corresponding to water) and the signs of a phlegmatic person, and then analyzes the role of natural heat versus ingested food (containing the four elements—fire, water, air, and earth, marked with colored alchemical triangles) and Galenic theory in generating the humors.

Concludes the preceding section on phlegmatic humours (left column) and introduces the melancholic complexion (right column) with a coloured portrait bust of Melancholia. Details the causes, physiological seats (spleen, mesenteric veins), physical symptoms, and psychological traits of melancholic individuals.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Von der Complexion der Melancholia.** (`#xywh=400,500,4628,1400`): Coloured portrait bust of a woman representing the melancholic complexion (Melancholia) in the upper half of the right column, framed by a black horizontal rule below. She has a pale, dusky-greyish complexion, heavy-lidded eyes, a yellow coif/headscarf, a black ribbon tied in a bow at her throat, and a muted mauve buttoned bodice.

Continues the account of the melancholic temperament, describing physical appearance, associated diseases (quartan fevers, cancer, leprosy), terrifying dreams, and the origin and distribution of black bile from the liver to the spleen. The second half of the right column introduces the three types of unnatural melancholic humours.

Discusses how a person's natural complexion can change over time due to diet, lifestyle, and environment, and explains how both the melancholic humour and the watery (phlegmatic) humour gain dominance. Concludes at the bottom of the right column with a new section defining phlegm (pituita) and its role in the four-humour balance.

Continuation of the treatise on phlegm (phlegma), its varieties, pathological effects (dropsy, lethargy, gout), and purgative/drying remedies (including squill vinegar and colocynth), followed by a new rubricated section on the origin, complexion, properties, and effects of the four humors (humidum nativum, blood, bile, phlegm), distinguishing natural from unnatural humors.

Continuation of the discussion of blood and the four humors, followed by a major rubricated section on the Complexions or Temperaments ('Von denen Complexionen oder Temperamenten'), explaining balanced (temperamentum ad pondus) versus imbalanced complexions, the eightfold division of complexions (four simple, four compound), and the specific complexions of individual organs.

Survey of the complexions of individual organs (veins, arteries, sinews, bones, heart, liver, flesh, spinal marrow, lungs) and the four ages of man (up to 18, 18–35, 35–49, and old age), accompanied by a small drawing of a handled flask/urinal (matula) in the right column; followed by a new rubricated section on the faculties/powers of the body ('Von den Khräfften. Vnd Was Krafft Sey'), introducing the animal/sensory, vital, and natural faculties.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Drawing of a handled flask (matula)** (`#xywh=900,500,4519,1400`): A small, lightly shaded ink/pencil sketch of a round-bellied glass vessel or urinal with a handle on the right, placed in the upper-middle of the right column alongside text discussing the expulsion of excess water/moisture in old age.

Exposition of the Galenic-humoral faculties (Kräfte): the vital faculty (Lebliche Krafft) seated in the heart and distributed via the arteries, and the natural faculty (Natürliche Krafft) seated in the liver, subdivided into generative, augmentative, and nutritive faculties. The right column details the four operations of nutrition (attraction, retention, digestion/coction, and expulsion) and how chyle is transformed into blood and bodily tissues.

Continuation on bodily excrements and digestion (sweat, vapor, hair, nails), followed by sections on the Natural Spirits (Spiritus Naturales, generated in the liver) and Vital Spirits (Spiritus Vitales, originating in the left ventricle of the heart). Illustrated with two anatomical human figures in the right column: one stippled in yellow showing an abdominal organ (liver/spleen), and one stippled in red showing the heart.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Figure of the Natural Spirits (Spiritus Naturales)** (`#xywh=900,500,4528,1400`): Full-length standing human figure stippled in yellow/ochre dots with arms slightly outstretched, depicting a dark reddish-brown organ in the upper abdomen.

**Figure of the Vital Spirits (Spiritus Vitales)** (`#xywh=900,500,4528,1400`): Full-length standing human figure stippled in red dots with arms slightly outstretched, depicting a prominent red heart in the center of the chest.

Discussion of the Vital Spirits (Spiritus Vitales), their arterial containment, origin from thin vapor and inhaled air, and corruption by pestilential air or obstruction. Followed by a section on the Animal/Sensory Spirits (Spiritus Animales), seated in the brain and distributed via the nerves, including an anatomical figure at the top right with raised arms and a highlighted brain.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Figure of the Animal Spirits (Spiritus Animales)** (`#xywh=400,500,4554,1400`): Full-length standing human figure stippled in red-brown dots with both arms raised in an upward posture, depicting a highlighted reddish-orange area at the crown of the head representing the brain.

Folio 283v discusses the vital and natural spirits implanted in the principal limbs, their inseparability from natural heat, and their role as instruments of the soul nourished by humorem radicalem. The right column features a full-length watercolor anatomical figure with outstretched arms, followed by a discussion of how breath-spirits are replenished and a major red rubricated heading introducing the powers and operations of the soul.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Full-length anatomical figure with outstretched arms** (`#xywh=900,500,4546,1400`): A standing, frontal nude human figure rendered in grey-blue and greenish watercolor wash with ink outlines and subtle yellow-gold highlights on the hands and chest, with arms extended horizontally and palms open.

Folio 284r continues the treatise on the soul, defining it as a heavenly, undivided essence and the true form of man that operates through the body's limbs. The right column enumerates its Latin designations (ratio, Mens, Animus, Sensus et intellectus) and classifies the four principal faculties of the soul: sensibility (empfindtligkheit), imagination (einbildung), judgment (Urtheill), and memory (gedächtnuß), beginning with an exposition of internal sensation.

Folio 285v continues the account of the internal senses, explaining how the five external senses converge into the common sense like lines to the center of a circle, and locating judgment in the third cell of the brain. It then treats fantasy/imagination (active even in sleep and dreams, and capable of moving the body in anger or joy) and, below a portrait bust of a curly-haired youth, introduces reason/judgment as the highest faculty of the soul.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Portrait bust of a curly-haired youth** (`#xywh=900,500,4545,1400`): A watercolor and ink illustration of the head and neck of a young person with golden-brown curly hair looking slightly downward, illustrating the seat of the internal senses, imagination, and reason in the head.

Recto folio 127 (page 286). Left column concludes a discussion of anger/passions and proceeds to a section on memory ('Nach der Vernunfft Volgt die gedechtnuß'), locating it in the cerebellum or fourth cell of the brain. Right column begins a major section on the division of the human body and its faculties ('Von abtheilung des menschen Leibs, Und Von der glider underscheidt'), classifying them into Animal (Seeliche), Vital (Leibliche), and Natural (Natürliche) powers.

Verso folio (page 287). Left column completes the division of bodily powers and introduces 'Von Wirkhung des Menschen' (Of the Operation of Man), distinguishing natural and voluntary operations. Right column continues with vital, natural (growth, generation, nutrition), and voluntary operations, and introduces the six non-natural things ('Res non naturales, oder nicht natürliche ding').

Recto folio 128 (page 288). Left column discusses the proper and improper use of the six non-natural things (citing Galen) and begins a major section on sleep ('Von den Schlaffen'). Right column treats the benefits of timely sleep, the harmfulness of midday sleep ('Der mittagige Schlaff ist Sehr schädlich'), optimal sleep duration (7–8 hours), diagnostic signs in urine and stomach after sleep, and begins a rubric on excessive waking.

Two-column medical treatise page continuing the discussion of passions (fear, bashfulness/shame, and anguish/trembling), followed by counsel for the physician to weigh age, sex, lifestyle, complexion, and season. The lower right column introduces the diurnal hours of the four humors (phlegm, blood, yellow bile, melancholy), illustrated with two red hourglass figures.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Two hourglass symbols** (`#xywh=400,500,4613,1400`): Two side-by-side red-ink hourglass figures drawn beneath the rubric on the diurnal movement of the four humors, symbolizing the measurement of the six-hour humoral periods.

**Lower 24-hour planetary and zodiacal wheel** (`#xywh=900,500,4540,1400`): Second large concentric circular table below the first, likewise divided into 24 hourly sectors with time-of-day labels ('Mitag', 'nach Mitag', 'Undergang', 'Miternacht', 'Nach miternacht', 'Vormitag') and concentric rings of planetary and zodiacal symbols.

Recto folio 292 opening the chapter on 'Melancolia. hipocontrica.' (Hypochondriac Melancholy). The upper left features a coloured ink-and-wash portrait of a melancholic man holding a staff and a celestial globe on a golden stand beside a four-paned window showing a starry night sky and crescent moon. The text describes the humoral etiology (burnt blood collecting in the mesenteric veins, affecting spleen, stomach, heart, and brain), physical symptoms (bloating, constipation, palpitations, dizziness, cold sweat), and behavioral manifestations (solitude, avoidance of company, devotion to reading and study).

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Melancolia. hipocontrica.** (`#xywh=400,500,4637,1400`): Coloured ink and wash illustration of a melancholic man wearing a dark cap, a rose-red capelet over an ochre robe, holding a staff in his right hand and a celestial globe mounted on a golden chalice-like stand in his left hand; behind him is a four-paned window overlooking a starry night sky with a crescent moon.

Verso folio 293, written in a single full-width column, continuing the treatise on hypochondriac melancholy. It discusses excessive sleep, heaviness of limbs, vertigo, tinnitus, diagnostic signs distinguishing spleen, liver, and stomach involvement, therapeutic principles (balancing a cold stomach with a hot liver, purgation, diet, and sweat-cures), and opens a new rubricated section on the effects of melancholia hypochondriaca.

Recto folio 294, arranged in two columns, continuing the account of the effects of melancholia hypochondriaca. It details the patient's changeable appetite, strange delusions, hemorrhoids ('guldine ader'), progression to chronic illness with quartan fever, and the physician's predicament—receiving blame, ingratitude, and slander from obstinate patients who constantly complain and change doctors. It concludes by identifying the primary cause as sour, foul moisture in the stomach from poor digestion, exacerbated by salted/spiced meats, sedentary habits, and excessive nocturnal study.

Page 295 (recto) discusses the pathophysiology of hypochondriacal melancholy, attributing it to unnatural fermentation in the intestines and acidity in the blood, and warns against bloodletting and overly harsh purges. It prescribes mild preparatory remedies (such as tincture of tartar and spirit of salt) and lists beneficial herbs and minerals. The right column features a watercolor illustration of four apothecary or drinking vessels on a shelf, followed by recipes for a decoction and a purgative draught for melancholy.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Four apothecary or drinking vessels on a shelf** (`#xywh=400,500,4531,1400`): A colored watercolor illustration in the right column depicting four vessels resting on a brown wooden shelf or table: a brown striped beaker, a blue-and-white ceramic pitcher with a handle, a blue-and-white stemmed goblet, and a small brown bowl.

Page 296 (verso) continues the recipe for the purgative draught and presents several further remedies for melancholy, black bile, and hypochondria: a purgative wine, a decoction for melancholy and black bile, a precious draught for hypochondria and internal melancholy, a powder for melancholy (with instructions for administration during the waning moon), a clyster (enema) for constipation and flatulence, and the beginning of a medicinal wine for obstructions of the spleen, liver, and stomach.

Page 297 (recto) completes the medicinal wine recipe and presents a sequence of gentle remedies for melancholy: strengthening lozenges (with a crossed-out bar below), pills, a safe purgative draught and divided powders, herbal sachets, a spleen-opening powder with steel extract, a precious syrup with apple juice, a chalybeate powder with prepared iron filings, and finally a springtime blood-purifying whey infusion.

Page 298 (recto) of Wellcome MS.990 contains early modern German and Latin medical recipes arranged in two columns, focusing on remedies for hypochondria, melancholy, flatulence, constipation, and blood purification. Treatments include borage flower infusions, rhubarb lozenges (Zeltl), a distilled spirit, blood-purifying herbal infusions, cheese-water (whey) infusions, a Maschanzker apple syrup with kermes or crimson silk for melancholy and heart palpitations, and purging little balls (Purgier Bälßel) to expel black bile and melancholic humors.

Page 299 (verso) of Wellcome MS.990 presents sudorific (sweating) remedies and laxative decoctions for purifying the blood and treating melancholy. The left column lists diaphoretic antimony and hartshorn powders, followed by a laxative draught of goat's milk whey, senna, and rhubarb, and a 20-day sarsaparilla and china-root decoction. The right column provides two complex herbal decoctions for stirring the spleen, liver, and mesenteric veins and evacuating burnt bile and phlegm, concluding with a gentle purging decoction of prunes, sebestens, jujubes, tamarinds, cassia, and manna.

Page 300 (recto) of Wellcome MS.990 opens in the left column with a small painted illustration of three red-filled bowls on a rectangular shelf beside the heading 'Absiesung des gebliedts' (Sweetening/tempering of the blood). The left column lists absorbent and blood-thinning remedies (crabs' eyes, corals, hartshorn, spirit of scurvy-grass, tincture of steel, and acidity-tempering herbs). The right column contains faded red rubrics for powders and pills with camphor and Peruvian balsam, a blood-purifying compound for severe conditions including leprosy and the Neapolitan disease (syphilis), and a concluding 'wonderful blood-purifying and expelling remedy' prepared as an electuary.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Three red-filled vessels on a tray** (`#xywh=400,500,4633,1400`): Small hand-colored illustration at the top left of the page beside the heading 'Absiesung des gebliedts', depicting three round golden-rimmed bowls or cupping vessels filled with a bright red substance (symbolizing blood) resting on a rectangular tan/wooden shelf or tray.

Page 302 (verso) contains a series of pharmaceutical recipes in Early New High German and Latin for purifying and sweetening the blood, treating melancholy, and cleansing the humors, primarily using fumitory (Fumaria), goat's milk whey, rhubarb, guaiacum (lignum sanctum), sarsaparilla, steel filings, and purgative syrups and powders.

Page 303 (recto) transitions from melancholy and blood purification to diseases of the spleen. The left column features an anatomical watercolor illustration of a spleen with its branching vessels, followed by a discussion of the shared remedies and physiological relationship between the liver and spleen, the obstruction of the portal vein, and the spleen's office of drawing melancholic humor. The right column describes symptoms of splenic illness (flatulence, vertigo, tinnitus, diaphragm oppression, chills, quartan fevers, inflammation) and their causes (over-eating, cold slimy food, drinking in heat, studying after meals).

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration on canvas 275** (`#xywh=400,500,4593,1400`): Watercolor and ink anatomical illustration of a bean-shaped reddish-brown spleen at the top of the left column, showing a branching blood vessel (splenic artery/vein) with three downward-extending roots emerging from the concave hilum to the left.

Page 304 (verso) lists materia medica and compound preparations beneficial for the spleen and liver. The left column categorizes herbs, roots, oils, gums, and aromatic tinctures that support the spleen and liver, dispel wind/flatulence, and temper/purify the humors. The right column outlines the therapeutic regimen: beginning with purgatives (rhubarb, aloes, agaric), followed by resolving steel/tartar powders, emetics if the stomach is slimy, and specific pill formulations (including Dr. Bontius's pills), steel-infused wine, and an aromatic confection.

Folio 305r contains recipes and treatments for spleen disorders, including tinctures and drops for blood circulation and flatulence, a decoction to open the spleen, oxymel and decoctions of ash bark to resolve splenic hardness, pills and plasters for spleen obstruction and quartan fever, and two ointments to soften and cool a hard, inflamed spleen.

Folio 307r concludes the section on spleen remedies with a powder for splenic hardening, features a colored anatomical illustration of the liver, gallbladder, and hepatic vessels, and begins a major chapter 'Von Kranckheit und Zuefellen der Leber' (On Sickness and Accidents of the Liver) discussing humoral causes, chyle, blood circulation, scirrhus, jaundice, colic, and general therapeutic principles.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Anatomical illustration of the liver and gallbladder** (`#xywh=400,500,4590,1400`): Hand-drawn ink and watercolor illustration in the middle of the left column depicting the lobed liver in reddish-brown, the pear-shaped gallbladder in yellow-green nestled beneath the lobes, and branching portal and hepatic vessels extending to the right and downward.

Folio 308v (two columns) contains Early New High German and Latin medical recipes for liver and spleen ailments, including purgative preparations with aloes, rhubarb, and agaricum, resolvents with cream of tartar and prepared steel, remedies for liver obstruction, precious liver powders, a rose confection (Confectio Rosarum) for heat of the liver, and the beginning of a decoction for a hot liver.

Folio 309r (two columns) continues the decoction for a hot liver and presents remedies for strengthening the liver, a red liver powder, a treatment for liver pains, and an extensive regimen for an overheated liver including syrups of chicory, borage, endive, and fumitory, bloodletting from the liver or salvatella vein, and purifying potions with whey.

Folio 310v (two columns) continues the purifying regimen with goat's milk whey and an opiate electuary, details the preparation of a precious coral tincture extracted with lemon or quince juice, recommends wild chicory and external poultices/fomentations for a hot liver, features a watercolor anatomical illustration of a liver with gallbladder and vessels above an empty label box, and begins a section on liver sickness from cold causes.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration on canvas 282** (`#xywh=900,500,4560,1400`): Hand-drawn watercolor and ink anatomical illustration of a two-lobed reddish-brown human liver with a yellowish-green gallbladder and greyish vessels/ducts, positioned above an uninscribed rectangular frame.

Unnumbered recto (preceding p. 312; small pencil '139' at bottom left) containing prescriptions for preparing and purging humors (mel rosatum, syrups of polypody, agrimony, eupatorium, and chicory, plus capon broth and pills), followed by a section on preparing 'Stachelwein' (steel/chalybeate wine) for obstructed liver and spleen, introduced by a drawn emblem combining an iron/key-like Mars symbol and the letter V.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Emblematic symbol above 'Wie man den Stachel Wein macht'** (`#xywh=400,500,4582,1400`): A hand-drawn, double-ruled rectangular frame containing an enlarged stylized alchemical/apothecary emblem: a blue-grey circle with a diagonal arrow/key-like shaft (Mars/iron symbol) beside a large shaded Roman letter V (for Vinum/wine).

Continues recipes for plasters and cerates to treat liver swellings and wind (flatulence), followed by a section on liver pain from wind and a new chapter (with a watercolor liver illustration) on inflammation and aposteme of the liver.

Details the treatment of liver apostemes via bloodletting, lenitives, syrups, external oils, and ripening cataplasms, followed by an illustration of a diseased liver and a new section on scirrhus (hardening) of the liver.

Concludes the treatment of liver scirrhus, presents an illustration of a bilobed liver, and begins a comprehensive chapter on 'Leber flus, oder Ruehr' (liver flux or dysentery), analyzing its causes, symptoms, and initial therapeutic approach.

Recipes and therapeutic instructions for treating an evil complexion of the liver and liver flux, including troches, electuaries, poultices, a calcined hare powder, and external spikenard and mastic oils.

Continued remedies for liver flux—including cooling species, astringent electuaries, a julep liquor, coral tincture, and an astringent plaster—followed by the opening section on lienteria (stomach flux).

Four-step cure for lienteria (diet, preparing humors, purging, and strengthening the stomach with laxatives, syrups, and external poultices), followed by various remedies for diarrhea and dysentery, including a solar-infused quince-juice secretum.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Shelf of five apothecary jars** (`#xywh=400,500,4569,1400`): Watercolor illustration in the middle of the right column depicting a wooden shelf holding five apothecary vessels: two red cylindrical albarelli, one tan cylindrical jar, and two blue globular jars.

Remedies for internal fluxes and ulcers using Armenian bole, comfrey, tormentil, oak bark, gum arabic, and Manus Christi, followed by the opening of a section on dysentery (Rotte Ruehr) accompanied by an illustration of a squatting figure.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Disenteria. Rotte Ruehr.** (`#xywh=900,500,4556,1400`): Color-washed pen-and-ink illustration in the lower right column depicting a man in a red tunic squatting outdoors beneath a leafy tree on grassy terrain, defecating bloody stool; a blank rectangular cartouche sits directly below the scene.

Etiology, prognosis, and dietary/therapeutic regimen for dysentery, warning against harsh purgatives like colocynth and scammony in favor of gentle laxatives, whey, cassia, tamarinds, and cooling syrups.

Continues the treatise on dysentery (Ruhr), detailing its prognosis across the four temperaments, internal remedies with rhubarb and theriac, a protective electuary, and the first of several clysters (enemas) illustrated with a syringe and clyster bladder.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Clyster syringe and bladder** (`#xywh=400,500,4583,1400`): Coloured pen-and-ink drawing in the right column depicting two clyster (enema) instruments: a cylindrical piston syringe with a central rod and nozzle on the left, and a blue-grey pear-shaped bladder attached to a curved cannula on the right, resting above a horizontal rectangular frame.

### Left Column

| Line | German Diplomatic (Original) | English Translation & Editorial Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |

| 3 | etlich dürt Stüell, so hat man ein frölich | some dry stools, thus one has a joyful |
| 4 | mitl in aller Arzeneifloß blüett ganz. | remedy in all medicine, [some] bleed completely. *— Note: Reading of 'Arzeneifloß' uncertain.* |

Continues with astringent and pain-soothing clysters for dysentery, followed by internal astringent simples, pediatric diarrhea treatments, and remedies for tenesmus (Zwang in der Ruhr) using fumigations, sitz baths, and herbal poultices.

Treats rectal prolapse (Außfall des Maßdarms) with astringent washes, oils, powders, and manual reduction, illustrated by a squatting figure; the lower right column introduces colic (Pasio Collica und Reißen) with a figure of a man clutching his abdomen.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Man squatting with rectal prolapse** (`#xywh=400,500,4582,1400`): Coloured pen-and-ink drawing at the top of the left column showing a man in a blue-grey tunic squatting on a green-yellow grassy hillock, illustrating rectal prolapse, above a horizontal rectangular frame.

**Man hunched with colic pain** (`#xywh=400,500,4582,1400`): Coloured pen-and-ink drawing in the lower right column showing a standing man in a reddish-brown coat, yellow breeches, and green stockings, hunched forward clutching his abdomen in pain, on a grassy hillock above a rectangular frame.

Continuation of clyster and suppository recipes for colic and intestinal wind, including an inline illustration of a tapered cylindrical suppository, followed by external abdominal anointing oils and fomentations.

Continuation of decoctions, plasters, and internal remedies for colic (including wolf's gut, almond oil, theriac, and chamomile in goat's whey), concluding with cautious instructions for using narcotic painkillers and opiate clysters when other measures fail.

Opens the chapter 'Von der Gelbsucht' (On Jaundice) with an illustrative bust portrait of a jaundiced woman, explaining its origin in biliary and hepatic obstruction and prescribing remedies including goose dung in milk, celandine, jalap resin, earthworms, saffron, and vervain.

Contains two short recipes (one an alchemical secretum using sublimated mercury for jaundice) in the upper left column, followed by an illustrated treatise 'Von der Wasersucht' (On Dropsy) depicting a dropsical man in bed and classifying dropsy into Ascites, Anasarca, and Tympanites.

**Von der Waser sucht** (`#xywh=900,500,4614,1400`): Pen-and-ink and watercolor illustration of a bearded man reclining on pillows in a bed with a red-patterned mattress and wooden frame, wearing a white shirt and red lower garment, with one hand resting on his distended abdomen (ascites/dropsy) and the other raised.

Continues the treatise on dropsy, detailing its etiology in faulty digestion (stomach, liver, and spleen), prognostic signs (good and fatal indicators regarding urine, coughing, diarrhea, and bleeding), and the danger of bloodletting, concluding with three primary causes of dropsy.

Continues poultice and plaster recipes for splenic and abdominal swelling using dung, slaked lime, sulphur, and urine, then introduces a new section on 'Winds Wasser sucht' (wind-dropsy/tympanites) with a hand-colored illustration of a seated patient.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Patient with Wind-Dropsy (Tympanites)** (`#xywh=900,500,4633,1400`): Hand-colored illustration at the top of the right column depicting a seated youth with curly brown hair wearing a red tunic and green lower garment against white and blue drapery, holding a round basin or distended form over the abdomen with the right hand while gesturing with the left.

Continues wind-dropsy treatments with pills and decoctions, an illustrated plaster recipe using blue iris root and ox dung, wind-expelling clysters, suppositories, a urine-based external remedy, and laxative infusions.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

Discusses the causes, symptoms, and varieties of internal winds (flatulence) affecting the stomach, chest, back, and kidneys, followed by recipes for wind powders, electuaries, lozenges, wind balls, and an external wind oil.

Continues recipes for wind oil and several distilled wind waters, then introduces a new section on diseases of the kidneys—specifically hot or inflamed kidneys—accompanied by an anatomical diagram of the kidneys and urinary vessels.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Anatomical diagram of the kidneys and urinary vessels** (`#xywh=900,500,4614,1400`): Hand-drawn ink and red wash diagram depicting two kidneys flanking two central vertical blood vessels (aorta and vena cava), with renal vessels and descending ureters below, framed above a horizontal rectangular bar.

Continues treatment for hot/inflamed kidneys with cooling emulsions, ointments, and clysters, discusses the hepatic origin of kidney stones (tartarous humors), and begins a new section on ulceration and putrefaction of the kidneys.

A continuation of a medical treatise on diagnosing purulent discharges from the kidneys, bladder, and prostate glands, followed by therapeutic recipes including a decoction, terebinth-based pills, a St. John's wort tincture/confection for expelling sand and gravel, and general remarks on treating kidney wounds.

A collection of pharmaceutical and medical recipes covering a carminative wind ointment, a uterine aqua, dropsy remedies, cordials for heart palpitations, an anodyne ointment, frostbite treatment, a mercury-ammoniacum plaster, and a chemical explanation of fixed and volatile alkalis.

This recto page contains Early New High German medical and apothecary recipes including a tincture of roses, two preparations of herbal tobacco for strengthening the head and memory, mouthwashes for oral ulcers and rotting gums, and fumigations and distilled wild thyme water for preventing head catarrhs.

This verso page records iatrochemical and surgical preparations, including Essentia Martis, Crocus Martis, an extract of lapis lazuli for vertigo and epilepsy, a gargle for loss of taste, pearl and coral cordials, an agglutinating wound powder (Pulvis glutinatoris) made from frogspawn, and remedies for pulmonary wind and bad breath.

Full-page watercolor illustration depicting the interior of an early modern apothecary and alchemical workshop, with a physician or apothecary preparing a remedy at a table while two friars present a prescription, and a distillation furnace in the foreground.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration on canvas 322** (`#xywh=900,500,4813,1400`): Full-page colored illustration of an apothecary workshop. Three upper shelves hold rows of red-labeled cylindrical jars, dark containers, and blue-and-white globular apothecary pots beside a four-pane window and a two-door wooden wall cabinet; an arched wooden door with iron strap hinges stands on the left. At a yellow-draped table, an apothecary in a pink-and-gold robe and feathered cap holds a red jar while stirring a coopered vat of red substance surrounded by jars, bottles, and a brass mortar and pestle. On the right, two tonsured friars in brown habits converse with him, one holding a small vial and handing over a written prescription (℞). On the checkered floor in the lower right sits a brick distillation furnace with glass retorts.

Continuation of the antimony diaphoreticum preparation (warnings on fumes, washing, dosage for gout, dropsy, and fever), followed by a further precious Antimony Diaphoreticum recipe using regulus of antimony, gold ducats, and a luted earthen vessel.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration on canvas 324** (`#xywh=900,500,4633,1400`): Small marginal ink-and-wash drawing in the right margin beside lines 22–24 depicting a cylindrical ribbed earthen vessel (haffen) and its domed lid (deckhel) for luting and reverberating the antimony powder.

Page 336 (verso) concludes the medical treatise on the virtues of a lunar diaphoretic remedy—praising its efficacy against fevers, plague, dropsy, gout, and melancholy—and continues with two alchemical recipes for preparing Tincture of Antimony, including a celebrated formulation attributed to a surgeon in Wels, Upper Austria.

Page 355 (recto) of Wellcome MS.990 contains the continuation and medicinal application of an antimonial tincture/oil (extracting Vitrum antimonii with vinegar, coagulating and resolving in a vapor bath until it becomes sweet as sugar), followed by a testimonial attributing the process to the author's son and two further recipes: preparing calcined antimony for the tincture and dissolving gold in a crucible to produce an oil of gold in a cellar.

Conclusion of the Oxy-Saccharum Emeticum recipe, followed by 'The Beautiful Treasure, Arcanum Corallinum' (mercurial preparation for syphilis/salivation), and steel/iron remedies including steel arcanum, artificial stone, steel tincture, and steely powder.

Page 364 verso contains Early New High German alchemical and medical recipes for preparing Crocus Martis (iron oxide) using sulfur and vinegar for treating chlorosis, jaundice, cramps, and dropsy, followed by recipes for another Crocus Martis, fixed Oleum Martis, and Turpethum Minerale (mercury sulfate).

Page 366 (verso) of MS.990 presents Early New High German alchemical and iatrochemical recipes arranged in two columns, including a salt of gold preparation for liver, spleen, and uterine complaints, an oil of tin (cinnabar/tin) remedy for the womb, a recipe for sugar of lead (Bley Zügflen), and a salt of copper (Sal Veneris) purgative.

Introduces medicinal and astrological properties of woods and roots, beginning with mistletoe wood, wintergreen, alder wood, oak mistletoe, ash wood (wound-wood), and peony root, detailing harvesting times by solar/lunar signs and therapeutic applications.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration of Mistletoe Tree** (`#xywh=400,500,4556,1400`): Hand-colored ink and watercolor drawing of a tree with a brown trunk and green-tinted foliage standing on a grassy mound, illustrating the section on mistletoe wood.

Concludes the treatise on natural and artificial mineral baths, detailing pre-bath purging and dietary regimens, gradual daily bathing schedules, post-bath sweating, and the stillicidium (head-dripping) therapy illustrated by a bather in a wooden tub.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration of Stillicidium (Head-Dripping Bath Therapy)** (`#xywh=400,500,4591,1400`): Hand-colored ink and watercolor illustration showing a person wearing a yellow headband/wreath sitting up to the shoulders in a round, hooped wooden bath tub filled with water, while a red wooden bucket suspended overhead drips water droplets from a brass-colored spout onto the bather's head.

Full-page colored illustration of a 17th-century apothecary and alchemical laboratory, showing an assistant grinding with a mortar and pestle amid shelves of albarelli and glass flasks, flanked by distillation furnaces.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Apothecary and Alchemical Workshop** (`#xywh=900,500,4643,1400`): Full-page colored ink and watercolor illustration depicting the interior of a 17th-century apothecary and alchemical laboratory. Shelves lined with red cylindrical albarelli jars and blue-tinted glass vessels wrap around the corner walls beneath a small paned window and yellow ceiling beam. At center, a young apothecary or assistant with long dark hair, wearing a red-and-gold doublet and yellow breeches, sits on a three-legged stool grinding substances with a pestle in a large mortar resting on a wooden block before a worktable holding jars and flasks. In the left foreground, a retort and receiver sit on a brick furnace; in the right foreground, a smaller alembic distillation apparatus sits over a portable stove and tripod on a checkered stone floor, while a figure peeks through a slightly ajar wooden door on the left.

A rubricated prefatory title introduces a treatise on distilling and preparing medicinal remedies, followed by instructions on digestion and circulation in flasks, cutting glass vessels, per descensum distillation, and distilling human blood. An ink-and-wash illustration at the bottom left (numbered 169) depicts three distillation vessels and a cubic furnace.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**169** (`#xywh=400,500,4552,1400`): Ink and watercolor illustration of three alchemical distillation apparatuses: at left, a round-bottomed retort/flask with a side spout and stopper; in the center, a tall pear-shaped cucurbit with a bulbous cap; at right, a cubic furnace or housing with a small spherical vessel protruding from the top.

Continues with chemical and medicinal distillation recipes, including making rectified spirits/acids, distilling honey, rectifying water without effort, distilling human blood, and preparing refreshing lemon, citron, bitter orange, and jasmine waters.

Continues the herbal water recipes, then presents several purgative and laxative waters (including the Queen's Water), two wondrous waters of great virtue with an extensive list of therapeutic uses, and two recipes for apoplexy water (Schlagwasser) using lily of the valley.

Page 381 (verso) contains Early New High German medical and alchemical recipes for distilled waters (Wasser, denoted by ▽) treating epilepsy (Fraiß), stroke (Schlag), headache, vertigo, stomach ailments, constipation, colic, and shortness of breath, followed by anise, cinnamon, and stroke waters.

Page 382 (recto) continues the recipe for stroke water, adds an epilepsy water prepared during the waning moon, and then presents a series of compound medical balsams (Schlag Balsam, Kaiser Leopolds Schlag Balsam, Frauen Schlag Balsam, Herzklopfen Balsam, Fluss Balsam, and Mutter Balsam) along with instructions on coloring balsams.

Page 383 (verso) concludes the instructions for coloring compound balsams and then presents several sulfur balsam preparations (Balsam Sulphuris, denoted by 🜍), including an asthma balsam, a potent sulfur balsam, a balsam for gangrene/necrosis, Martin Ruland's Balsam Sulphuris for surgical wounds and hemorrhoids, and a Balsam Vitae.

Page 384 (recto) opens with a recipe for a wound basilicon balm for internal and external conditions, followed by a color illustration of a clyster syringe and a new rubricated section on various clysters. The right column contains clyster prescriptions for apoplexy, lethargy, vertigo, head illnesses, and paralysis.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Clyster syringe** (`#xywh=400,500,4490,1400`): Pen-and-ink and watercolor illustration of a yellow-brown cylindrical clyster syringe with a detached pointed nozzle on the left and a plunger handle on the right, resting above a narrow strip of green grass.

Page 386 (recto) concludes the clyster balm recipe, followed by a large watercolor illustration of two pots boiling on a hearth fire with an attendant carrying a jug. Below a red-and-cream decorative divider, a new rubricated section on decoctions begins, including rooster decoctions for belly pain and liver/spleen obstructions, and decoctions for wind, bile, and fumitory.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Two pots boiling over a hearth fire with an attendant carrying a jug** (`#xywh=400,500,4525,1400`): Pen-and-ink and watercolor illustration of two brown earthen pots boiling over a wood fire with red flames and rising smoke on a rectangular masonry hearth; to the right, a standing figure in a grey coat, yellow tunic, and red breeches holds a red pitcher in a doorway. A decorative red-and-cream striped horizontal bar separates the illustration from the text below.

This verso page (numbered 387) contains medicinal decoction recipes (Decocta) organized by season—spring, summer, and autumn—as well as preparations for wounds, fistulas, a purgative 'Decoctum Solutiuo Catholico', and a guaiacum wood decoction ('Decotum de lig: sanctum').

This recto page (numbered 388) features two colored pen-and-ink illustrations of apothecary vessels and wine goblets, alongside recipes for cooling and laxative emulsions ('Emulsian oder Melaun Milch') and medicinal wines ('Tamarisken Wein', 'Laxier Wein').

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Three apothecary vessels on a wooden shelf (Left Column)** (`#xywh=400,500,4525,1400`): Colored pen-and-ink drawing depicting two cylindrical shaded beakers/tumblers and one handled pitcher/jug resting on a tan wooden ledge above the heading 'Emulsian oder Melaun Milch'.

**Goblet with red wine and cylindrical jar on a shelf (Right Column)** (`#xywh=400,500,4525,1400`): Colored pen-and-ink drawing depicting a stemmed glass goblet filled with dark red liquid beside a cylindrical grey jar/box on a tan and reddish-brown shelf above the heading 'Von Ender hierlichen Wein'.

Page 390 opens with a recipe for a laxative wine, followed by a rubricated treatise on the art of targeted purging—explaining how purgatives like agaric act on specific organs (head, liver, spleen, stomach, chest) and how corrective herbs must be added to protect healthy organs. The upper right column features a colored illustration of an apothecary shop, beneath which the text lists simples that draw to and strengthen the head.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Apothecary Shop Scene** (`#xywh=400,500,4507,1400`): Colored pen-and-ink and watercolor illustration occupying the upper half of the right column. Two upper shelves hold rows of red and yellow-and-blue apothecary jars (albarelli); two lower shelves hold red and green jars. Behind a wooden counter draped with a green-and-yellow cloth stands a woman in a pink bodice, white kerchief, and yellow skirt, gesturing toward a bearded man in a brown robe with bare feet who holds a small dark cup. Four red cylindrical jars, a dark square box, and a dark jug rest on the counter.

Page 391 catalogs medicinal simples organized by the organs they serve: liver, chest, spleen, kidneys/loins, stomach, bladder/stones, and womb. The right column continues with general rules on administering purgatives according to age, constitution, and season, and begins a section on mild purgative remedies.

Page 392 classifies moderate and strong purgatives as well as mild and strong emetics, followed by instructions on recognizing good scammony and its six harmful effects, and the medicinal virtues of larch agaric. The right column describes the preparation of larch agaric troches and summarizes the properties and humoral degrees of turbith, rhubarb, rhapontica, mechoacanna, and hermodactyl.

Page 393 presents an illustrated materia medica entry on five varieties of myrobalans (Belleric, Emblic, Chebulic, Indian, and Citrine) with their humoral properties and dosages, followed by a rubricated section on preparatory syrups for purging bile, phlegm, and melancholic humours.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**1. Myrobalanj Bellerica.** (`#xywh=900,500,4667,1400`): Wash-shaded ink drawing of an oval Belleric myrobalan fruit with a short stem at the top.

**2. Myrobalanj Emplicj.** (`#xywh=900,500,4667,1400`): Wash-shaded ink drawing of a ribbed, segmented Emblic myrobalan fruit.

**3. Myrobalanj Chebula.** (`#xywh=900,500,4667,1400`): Wash-shaded ink drawing of an elongated, pear-shaped Chebulic myrobalan fruit with a stem at the top.

**4. Myrobalanj Indica.** (`#xywh=900,500,4667,1400`): Wash-shaded ink drawing of a smaller, rounded-teardrop Indian myrobalan fruit with a stem at the top.

**5. Myrobalanj Citrinj.** (`#xywh=900,500,4667,1400`): Wash-shaded ink drawing of a large, oval-pyriform Citrine myrobalan fruit with a short neck at the top.

| :---: | :--- | :--- |

Early New High German medical-pharmaceutical recipes for laxative waters, a bile potion, laxative milk, quince juice, a laxative potion, and several laxative electuaries using senna, rhubarb, jalap, scammony, and manna.

Early New High German medical recipes for laxative lozenges (morselli) and tablets (Zeltel), followed by topical laxative plasters and ointments applied to the belly or navel, including remedies for children.

Continuation of topical laxative ointments followed by numerous recipes for laxative powders (Laxier Pulver) using jalap resin, scammony, cream of tartar, hermodactyl, and turbith, including a child and bile powder attributed to the apothecary of Leoben.

Introduces a secret collection of noble pill recipes with an explanatory discourse on purging the three bodily humors (phlegm, choler, melancholia), followed by an illustration of a pillbox and two pill recipes for strengthening the senses and preserving the body from putrefaction.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration on canvas 364** (`#xywh=900,500,4655,1400`): Watercolor and ink drawing of a round, flat cylindrical yellow-ochre pillbox or apothecary container with a dark lid rim resting on a brown shelf or table surface.

Presents pill recipes for lientery/white dysentery (marked with a pointing hand), chest and lung diseases, toothache, obstructions (Pilulae de opilata), dropsy, and five distinct recipes for head and eye pills.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Illustration on canvas 366** (`#xywh=900,500,4697,1400`): Small ink drawing of a pointing hand (manicule) with a cuff in the top-left margin beside the page number 402, pointing right toward the rubricated heading 'Pillule für Lienteria oder Weisse rüehr.'.

Folio 403r contains twelve pharmaceutical pill recipes in Early New High German and Latin, targeting quartan fever, uterine prolapse, constipation, kidney stones, sciatica, headaches, and sharp humors. The page is arranged in two columns with rubricated red-ink headings and frequent apothecary and alchemical symbols.

Folio 404v introduces a new section on 'noble powders' (Edlen Puluer), headed by a watercolor illustration of four red cylindrical apothecary jars on a shelf. It records six recipes for cordial, cooling, and warming gemstone, pearl, and epilepsy powders in Early New High German and Latin.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Four apothecary jars on a shelf** (`#xywh=900,500,4698,1400`): Watercolor illustration at the top of the left column depicting four red cylindrical apothecary vessels/jars with rims standing in a row on a brown shelf against a plain background.

Folio 405r continues the collection of medicinal powders, including an arcanum for pregnant women against epilepsy, a head-bag powder, a carminative stomach powder, a heart-strengthening powder, two epilepsy powders, and astrological instructions for digging peony root. Rubricated red-ink headings and alchemical/astrological symbols appear throughout.

Page 406v presents medicinal treatises on the virtues of dissolved pearls (compared to aurum potabile), a disclosure exposing counterfeit stag's heart-bones (Hirschkreuzel) substituted with ox-heart bones, and recipes for hartshorn jelly (Hirschsulze) and Magisterium of hartshorn, accompanied by a hand-colored illustration of a leaping stag.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Leaping stag** (`#xywh=900,500,4730,1400`): Hand-colored ink and watercolor illustration of a brown stag with antlers leaping to the left across green grassy terrain, framed below by a red ink horizontal line.

Page 407r concludes the Magisterium of hartshorn and presents an illustrated alchemical treatise on distilling philosophical hartshorn with cooling and cordial herbs (chicory, endive, sorrel, scorzonera, blessed thistle, lemon balm, borage) over five days to produce a restorative jelly for hot fevers.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Distillation apparatus and furnace** (`#xywh=400,500,4493,1400`): Hand-colored ink and watercolor illustration of an alchemical distillation setup: a brick furnace on the right topped with a copper alembic whose spout leads to a large brown receiver vessel resting on a wooden stand on the left, with a small black pot underneath and a building with a smoking chimney in the background.

Page 410 (verso) contains alchemical and workshop recipes in two columns, covering the preparation of gum pastilles (Gumj.), boiled oil (Faum öll.), pitch (Pöch), iron slag pigment (Scoria feri), calcined ivory (Helffen bain), a clarifying preparation (Heider Plätt zu L:), and a rubricated treatise on artificial gemstones (Edl stain Allerleÿ zu L:).

Page 411 (recto) continues an alchemical procedure for calcining, reverberating, and extracting gemstones with spiritus and vinegar, followed by a rubricated section on the medicinal virtues of oil of gemstones. The right column concludes a reference to Hieronymus Bock's Herbarium and presents two rubricated sections detailing the virtues of dissolved pearls and the method for dissolving pearls, corals, and crabs' eyes using lemon juice or spiritus and salt spirit.

Page 412 presents a colored illustration of a distillation furnace and alembic followed by recipes for distilling herbal and floral spirits (scurvy-grass, elderberry, rose, wormwood, lily of the valley), a uterine spirit (Muetter Geist), and the beginning of a saffron elixir.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Distillation apparatus** (`#xywh=0,0,5997,6853`): Colored drawing of a brick distillation furnace with an open firebox showing red flames, surmounted by a metallic or grey alembic with a long descending spout leading into a spherical glass receiver resting on a low four-legged stand.

Page 414 concludes the sugar of roses recipe and presents an illustrated treatise on the virtues, extracts, and purgative preparations of black hellebore (Schwarze Nieswurz) for hypochondria, gout, epilepsy, and dropsy, followed by an arcanum for longevity.

Folio 415r presents a botanical illustration of Bryony root (Prijonia Wurzl) accompanied by a rubricated treatise on its purgative virtues against dropsy, chest phlegm, and uterine suffocation. The right column provides three compound extract recipes with apothecary weights, dosage instructions, and a rubricated NB warning on the milder potency of Bryony fecula.

Folio 416v concludes the Bryony remedies with lozenge and uterine potion recipes, followed by a rubricated section on testing the purity of a chemical salt or nitre (marked with a circled 1) by burning it on a hot iron plate. The remainder of the page details the therapeutic uses of this preparation against malignant fevers, plague, kidney stones, liver obstruction, and throat inflammation.

An unnumbered recto folio featuring a full-page hand-colored illustration of an apothecary's workshop, showing a bearded monk in a brown habit holding a red flask behind a table laden with a mortar and pestle, vials, and boxes beneath four shelves of apothecary jars. The lower-right portion of the illustration is covered by a large blank paper repair patch, with modern pencil foliation 188 in the bottom-left corner.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Apothecary's workshop with monk** (`#xywh=0,0,5822,6853`): Full-page watercolor and ink illustration depicting four shelves of green, yellow, and terracotta apothecary jars above a leaded window, a yellow wall cabinet with black hinges, and a bearded monk in a brown habit holding a small red flask behind a red-draped table with a brass mortar and pestle, glass vials, and boxes; a distillation vessel sits at far left, and a large blank paper patch covers the lower-right half.

Verso folio (p. 418) opening a section on medicinal and alchemical oils, including a rubricated preface, a recipe for citron and bitter orange oil (partially obscured by a blank paper patch in the left column) illustrated with a watercolor distillation flask in the right column, followed by recipes for Oleum septem florum and Oleum anodynum (bryony oil).

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Distillation vessel (gläßl) for separating essential oils from water** (`#xywh=0,0,6045,6853`): Watercolor and ink illustration of a round blue-gray glass flask/receiver resting on a brownish-green mound with small yellow plant tufts, showing a narrow neck with a small attached side-receptacle or stopper at the top.

Page 421 contains Early New High German apothecary recipes for purgative extracts and electuaries, including a bryony extract, a gentle purgative electuary safe for pregnant women and children, a polypody-senna electuary, a complex turpeth-colocynth electuary against syphilis and phlegm, and an iron-based electuary for spleen and liver obstructions.

Page 422 records cordial and pectoral remedies, including electuaries for heart palpitations, bilious disorders, and chlorosis (green-sickness) in maidens, an aromatic heart sachet, a syrup of quince and camomile oil, and a complex pectoral juice for lung obstructions and asthma.

Page 423 features remedies for asthma, phthisis, tertian fever (including pulse plasters), a laxative cataplasm, and two procedures for purifying and distilling turpentine, accompanied by a colored drawing of a wooden filtration vessel.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Wie Man den Terpenthin Leütern sol (Turpentine Purification Vessel)** (`#xywh=0,0,5804,6853`): Colored ink and wash illustration in the upper-middle of the right column depicting a golden-yellow cylindrical linden-wood container (Pixen) resting atop a grey-blue cylindrical receiving vessel/glass on a brown wooden block, illustrating the filtration of turpentine.

Contains recipes for floral and herbal tinctures, honeys, juleps, and juices (rose, violet, elderberry, mulberry, raspberry, scurvy-grass), followed by medicinal virtues of the common elder tree and elder syrup, illustrated with a rose blossom and an elder tree.

**Rose blossom (Rosen Tinctur / Rosen Hönig)** (`#xywh=0,0,5803,6853`): Small hand-colored botanical drawing in the left column depicting a pink/red rose blossom with green leaves and a brown stem.

Continues the elder syrup recipe and gives preparations of elder water and elder bark emetics/purgatives; the right column presents recipes for hair removal, a water-igniting stone, tartar emetic, balsam of sulfur, a melancholy sachet, and good ink, illustrated with a nettle sprig and an inkstand.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Nettle sprig (Das khain har Wachse)** (`#xywh=0,0,6024,6853`): Small hand-colored botanical drawing in the right column depicting a leafy sprig (likely Urtica/nettle) with yellowish-green leaves.

**Inkstand with quill pen (Guette Dintten Machen)** (`#xywh=0,0,6024,6853`): Small hand-colored drawing in the lower right column showing a cylindrical red-brown pot and a dark inkwell with a quill pen resting on a wooden desk.

Folio 427r contains recipes for black writing inks, Spanish sealing wax, grass-root water for dropsy and jaundice, and two preparations of purging and medicinal wormwood wine.

Folio 429r concludes the fragrant cap-powder recipe and presents remedies for cress mucilage, heart cordials, vinegar making, an illustrated arum-root preparation (Jerja Serpentaria), ant oil for sciatica, and lozenges for melancholy.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Arum maculatum (Lords-and-Ladies / Cuckoo-pint)** (`#xywh=0,0,5858,6853`): Hand-colored botanical illustration in the upper-left margin of the right column showing three green leaves, a drooping bell-like flower in blue and yellow, and fibrous roots below.

**Red-ink heart ornaments** (`#xywh=0,0,5858,6853`): Two small solid red-ink heart symbols centered beneath the rubricated headings 'In Hizigen frenen beÿ dem' and 'Ain Herliche Hertz Stärckung.' in the left column.

**Red-ink wheel emblem** (`#xywh=0,0,5858,6853`): A small circular eight-spoked wheel or rosette drawn in red ink beneath the rubricated heading 'Zeltel für die Melancholischen Wind' in the right column.

Page 430 (verso) contains alchemical and medical recipes, including a gold solution for uterine ailments, depilatory and hair-retention ointments, cements for repairing broken glass and majolica vessels, a tincture of sal tartari for stomach and bile, a cephalic snuff powder, and a protective charm/ointment against gunfire.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Bust portrait of a young man in profile** (`#xywh=0,0,6029,6853`): Framed watercolor and pen-and-ink illustration in the left column beside the hair-loss recipes, showing a young man in profile facing left with wavy light-brown hair, wearing a red tunic with a wide yellow-ochre collar.

Page 431 (recto) features three medical-alchemical recipes in the left column (a gold-based resolvent for fevers, a sudorific extract, and a mercury precipitate) and an illustrated treatise on boiling good soap in three or four hours in the right column.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Soap-boiler at a furnace with a wooden lye tub** (`#xywh=0,0,5811,6853`): Framed watercolor and pen-and-ink illustration at the top of the right column depicting a man in a green tunic, black cap, and red breeches standing beside a brick hearth with a fire burning under a round cauldron, sprinkling powder while stirring with a rod; to the right stands a large hooped wooden tub on three legs.

Continuation of recipes for urinary fluxes, sudorifics, and urethral injections, followed by an illustrated section on external remedies for scabby head (Erbgrind / tinea capitis).

Collection of Early New High German and Latin recipes including a secret mercurial water for putrefaction, a bile draught, a laxative bolus, a strengthening electuary, sudorific and fever remedies, hematuria, uterine fumigation, insomnia, and cosmetic paint.

### Illustrations and Anatomical Diagrams

**Small fluted vessel above Gall Tränckel** (`#xywh=0,0,5787,6853`): Small hand-drawn, blue-tinted conical cup or fluted vessel positioned above the 'Gall Tränckel' heading in the left column.

Verso folio 440 containing recipes for an old wound plaster using Lapis campestris and oil, a heart-strengthening essence of hart's-tongue (Hirschensprengel), a balsam of human blood for apostemes and wounds, Lac Sulphuris (milk of sulfur), a common cough and hemoptysis potion, and a laxative potion.

Recto folio 441 containing a vinegar preparation, remedies and natural antidotes against evil spirits and demonic possession (using St. John's wort, peony, coral, etc.), treatments for excess black bile (melancholy), and distilled waters for restoring reason, melancholy, and strengthening the head and heart.
